title: 100% renewables is doable, even in oil countries - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Oil- and gas-producing countries could strengthen their economies by accelerating domestic renewable energy deployment while maintaining fossil fuel exports, according to LUT University professor Christian Breyer. In an interview with
pv magazine
, he pointed to Norway as an example of how electrification can maximize the economic value of fossil fuel resources, while arguing that Russia’s political choices are preventing it from exploiting similar opportunities.
Emiliano Bellini
19 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Expanding renewable energy is not necessarily at odds with the economic interests of countries that depend heavily on oil and gas exports. On the contrary, replacing fossil fuels in domestic energy consumption with renewable electricity could allow these countries to increase export revenues while developing cleaner and more efficient energy systems at home.
These are the findings of a new study conducted by researchers at LUT University in Finland, who identified Norway as a particularly successful example of this approach. The country has combined substantial oil and gas production with extensive renewable electricity generation, widespread electric vehicle adoption, and increasing electrification of heating.
“The most clever oil and gas producing countries do so, see
,” Christian Breyer, professor for Solar Economy at Finland’s LUT University, told
pv magazine
, referring to investments in renewable energy and electrification.
He explained that reducing domestic fossil fuel consumption allows exporting countries to retain more of their oil and gas production for international markets. At the same time, electrification can improve the efficiency of domestic energy use and reduce emissions. “This allows them to export more fossil fuels whereas domestically they have a highly efficient and clean energy system,” he said, describing the strategy as economically advantageous.
However, Breyer argued that Norway remains an exception rather than the rule. Many fossil fuel exporters have yet to fully exploit the economic opportunities associated with their energy resources, particularly when it comes to developing renewable electricity generation and electrifying domestic demand.
The development of renewable energy in fossil fuel-exporting economies does not necessarily send contradictory signals to importing countries, according to Breyer. He noted that several Middle Eastern countries have begun investing in large-scale solar PV projects without undermining their oil and gas export businesses.
In his view, the continued demand for fossil fuels is largely independent of whether producing countries accelerate their own energy transitions. He compared fossil fuel dependence to other forms of addiction, arguing that consumers may continue purchasing products despite being aware of their long-term economic and environmental costs.
The situation in
presents a markedly different picture. Although the country has developed some solar and wind power capacity, renewable energy deployment has remained relatively limited compared with its resource potential. The expansion of the sector has also stalled since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Breyer suggested that Russia could, in principle, benefit from the same strategy pursued by Norway and increasingly considered by other fossil fuel-producing economies, including countries in the Middle East, the United States, and Canada.
Such a transition could reduce domestic fossil fuel consumption and create additional economic value from the country’s energy resources. Greater deployment of distributed renewable energy systems could also contribute to electricity supply diversification and, with appropriate grid design and storage, improve resilience against disruptions.
However, Breyer sees the main obstacles as political rather than technological or economic. He is skeptical that international sanctions or Russia’s increasing technological dependence on China would, by themselves, fundamentally change the country’s renewable energy prospects. Instead, he argued that progress would depend on policy decisions prioritizing long-term national economic interests.
“It would require clever policy making to the advantage of the country and its people,” he said.
Breyer was particularly critical of the economic and human consequences of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, arguing that the destruction of economic value, loss of life, and damage to the country’s international reputation illustrate the consequences of political decisions that run counter to long-term national interests.
“Rational advantageous choice are often not considered if irrational ruling is prevailing,” he said.
For Breyer, the contrast between Norway and Russia illustrates a broader challenge facing fossil fuel-exporting countries. Their resource wealth provides an opportunity to finance renewable energy deployment, electrify domestic energy systems, and improve economic efficiency. Whether that opportunity is realized ultimately depends on political priorities and the willingness of governments to pursue long-term economic benefits.
Breyer and his colleagues presented the results of their research in the paper “
Sustainable energy transition options for Russia
,” published in
Energy Reports

title: Swift Current alleges widespread module defects in lawsuit against First Solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Massachusetts-based developer filed a complaint in the New York supreme court that alleges the module manufacturer knew about defects that have caused underperformance in more than 2.4 million modules it delivered to Swift Current sites in 2023 and 2024.
Ben Zientara
19 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Double Black Diamond Solar project in Illinois.
Renewable energy developer Swift Current Energy is suing First Solar in New York state court, alleging the manufacturer knowingly supplied defective solar modules and used deceptive testing to hide significant performance issues.
The complaint, filed in Sept. 2026, alleges that First Solar supplied over 2.4 million defective Series 6 Plus and Series 7 thin-film cadmium telluride modules across three major U.S. solar installations, including the
800 MW Double Black Diamond project
in Illinois.
The developer states it paid more than $360 million for the equipment, which it claims has consistently failed to meet promised power output metrics.
According to the complaint, the modules experienced increased degradation and significantly lower-than-expected output immediately upon installation in 2023 and 2024. Swift Current says it initially submitted formal warranty claims on Dec. 23, 2024, after discovering the widespread underperformance.
First Solar formally responded on May 2, 2025, stating that the developer had not adequately described or provided evidence of the claimed defects, and noted that evaluating power output claims based on system-level performance data is invalid under the warranty terms.
The module maker requested that Swift Current coordinate with its technical support to conduct individual module power output measurements in a laboratory. Swift Current’s court filing called this proposed remedy “commercially impossible,” arguing it would require shipping more than 1.5 million modules back to First Solar at a cost exceeding the value of the claims.
In the complaint, Swift Current points to its inability to meet commitments to its commercial offtakers under power purchase agreements as a result of the power output loss. In addition, the developer says it has lost revenue from decreased compensation under capacity contracts it signed for two of the projects in question.
Defect allegations
Swift Current claims that First Solar identified two primary errors in its manufacturing process that led to lower power output in 1.6 million of the modules it purchased from the module maker.
The developer alleges First Solar knew about the defects at the time it shipped modules to its sites, but concealed them from the developer until October 2024. Importantly, one of the defects alleged in the complaint appears never to have been publicly acknowledged by the module maker.
The first type of these errors, which Swift Current calls “Edge Grind Defects” is related to a flaw in the manufacturing process for Series 7 modules first publicly disclosed by First Solar in an Oct. 2024 earnings call.
In the call, First Solar CEO Mark Widmar provided details how the company identified the issue early in Series 7 production, in which materials that have been ground from the edge of module glass “calcify” onto the glass during the “dwell time” between the grinding step and a module washing step that occurs after.
At the time, First Solar said it had identified and taken actions to address the edge grind issues and was taking a warranty charge of $50 million in anticipation of providing service to buyers of affected modules.
The second, previously-undisclosed type of defect is referred to in the complaint as “Substrate Defects,” which Swift Current alleges arose from a change to the manufacturing process initiated by First Solar in 2021, which prevented the absorber layer for its Series 6 Plus and 7 modules from forming as designed. The complaint states these defects “impacted the annealing process, film quality, recombination rates, and ultimately, module power output.”
Swift Current says it was presented with an investigative report First Solar commissioned from Leidos Engineering, LLC to examine its Series 7 modules, which identifies the two defects being present in the modules. The complaint says the Leidos report found an average power loss of approximately 8 percent for modules tested after nearly one year of field deployment.
The complaint also goes further, alleging “metastability losses inherent in First Solar’s thin film cadmium telluride technology,” which can result in seasonal loss of power output during cold periods of the year.
Swift Current alleges that First Solar artificially inflates its modules’ nameplate power ratings using a secret, proprietary “preconditioning” testing method that masks the metastability loss by testing module power output immediately after subjecting the panels to at least eight hours of extreme heat, voltage and irradiance.
The complaint says that while the edge grind and substrate defects were present in more than 1.6 million of the modules it received, all 2.4 million failed to perform as promised, with the alleged metastability issues solely at fault for lower-than expected production from the remaining modules.
Swift Current is seeking damages and restitution due to the alleged defects. In addition, it has asked the New York court to apply penalties under a Massachusetts law regarding willful misconduct, because the Swift Current employees who evaluated the modules and negotiated the deal to purchase them are based at the company’s headquarters in Massachusetts and the commercial relationship between the two companies was managed there.
The case is active and ongoing, with the parties scheduled to appear before Justice Andrew Borrok of the New York county commercial division of the New York state supreme court on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Living bacteria and sand used to make eco-friendly cement without heat
content: To build the sustainable cities, scientists at ETH Zurich are turning to some of the smallest living organisms on Earth. Dr. Karen Antorveza Paez, an architect and researcher, has merged biology with digital fabrication, using living bacteria, sand, and robotics to manufacture solid architectural components without burning a single fossil fuel. The development targets one of the planet’s biggest environmental culprits. Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of global carbon emissions, largely because key ingredients must be fired in massive kilns at extreme temperatures.Antorveza Paez skips the heat entirely. And recruits Sporosarcina pasteurii, a soil bacterium capable of producing “mineral glue”. “We use bacteria to produce a kind of mineral adhesive,” Antorveza Paez noted.  A robotic arm repeatedly applies bacteria, the substances necessary for calcification, and sand to a surface, allowing it to grow layer by layer. (Image: Gerhard Bliedung / ETH Zurich)No kilns requiredMicrobially induced calcium carbonate precipitation allows living bacteria to bond sand and loose grains into solid structural components without high-heat processing. Although the idea is not new, experts have previously considered this approach to build structures on Mars. Bacterial breakdown of urea via a natural enzyme produces carbonate ions within the mixture. When they interact with calcium chloride, these ions form microscopic limestone crystals that mechanically interlock sand grains and solidify the material at room temperature.“It’s a bit like baking a cake,” Antorveza Paez explained. “You have the dough, which is still very malleable and fragile. Only the oven turns it into something solid.” In her work, the bacteria take on the role of the oven. The team developed two digital manufacturing methods to create biocement architectural elements. Researchers developed a 3D bio-printing process for biocement elements using a custom bio-ink made of water, natural gums, sand, and live bacteria. Once printed into shape, the structure undergoes a two-to-five-day mineralization bath that is refreshed daily to supply necessary nutrients. Like an oven, the bacteria cure the material at room temperature without external heat, leaving a fully solidified, inactive mineral component after drying.Strength challenge remains The second approach uses a robotic arm to spray alternating layers of sand, bacteria, and mineralizing agents onto surfaces, drawing inspiration from natural microbial rock structures like stromatolites.“As an architect, you usually don’t know exactly what’s in a material – it’s manufactured somewhere else,” she said. “I’m fascinated by the fact that nature has found ways to produce highly sophisticated materials, and that we can use this to address our current problems.” It is a promising approach. But biocement is not yet ready to replace structural concrete. Currently, its strength is closer to mortar, making it better suited for non-load-bearing elements like partition walls or facade panels.Furthermore, the chemical reaction releases ammonium, a polluting byproduct that must be safely treated or recycled.“Unless we consider the disposal of this chemical byproduct, building with biocement is unfortunately not sustainable,” added Antorveza Paez. Demonstrating the potential for automated construction, a six-month installation at the Venice Architecture Biennale 2025 showed a biocement structure growing live in front of visitors.Scientists have already proven that bacteria can grow building materials. Now, the race is on to make those materials strong enough to support our cities.

title: Tiny worm brains reveal surprising sex differences beyond neural wiring
content: With 302 neurons, 200 of them in their heads, hermaphrodite female roundworms reveal surprising sex-specific differences in the nervous system and how these differences influence behavior, reproduction, and aging. Researchers at Northeastern University compared brain activity in male and hermaphroditic Caenorhabditis elegans, a microscopic worm widely used in biological research to understand how sex wires males and female nervous systems differently. Their study, published in Current Biology, showed that nearly every chemosensory neuron in a tiny roundworm responds differently to at least one chemical signal depending on the animal’s sex, “indicating that sexually dimorphic circuits are pervasive and stimulus-dependent,” the researchers wrote in the study.As male and hermaphroditic nervous systems revealed widespread differences in how they process information, the lead researcher told Northeastern that their central question concerned how brain structure relates to brain function. Mapping sex differences across the brainAt 1 millimeter long, transparent hermaphrodites Caenorhabditis elegans have 302 neurons throughout their nervous systems, while males have approximately 387, according to Northeastern University.Vivek Venkatachalam, an associate professor of physics at Northeastern University, explained that the worms are primarily chemosensory animals. They rely heavily on smell and taste. Researchers monitored individual neurons as worms encountered chemical stimuli, including odors, salt, and pheromones. Using calcium imaging, a technique that measures changes in calcium levels inside neurons, they tracked changes in neural activity across the animals’ heads.The team found that sensory responses varied between sexes and also depending on the stimulus.“We’ve known for a while that the male and hermaphrodite worm nervous systems are wired somewhat differently, but a wiring diagram only tells you so much about how a brain actually works,” said Javier Apfeld, a Northeastern associate professor of biology, said in the Northeastern report.The team found that sensory responses varied not only by sex but also by stimulus, identifying sex-specific responses in neurons associated with feeding and digestion.“This dimorphic and monomorphic activity was present to a lesser extent in downstream interneurons and even less so in motoneurons, implicating sensory neurons as the primary source and location of sexually dimorphic activity,” the researchers reported.The researchers also investigated whether differences in neural activity corresponded to differences in the physical connections between neurons. Scientists compared the worms’ observed neural activity with previously published maps of synaptic connections, or connectomes. The researchers found that functional differences in neurons were distinct from differences in their physical connections.In other words, researchers investigated whether neural activity corresponded to the physical connections between neurons. They found that structural differences did not predict functional changes.“Comparing the functional activity we measured to the published synaptic connectomes of both sexes revealed that sexual dimorphism in functional connectivity was distinct from and complementary to sexual dimorphism in synaptic connectivity,” the study stated.The findings could provide a foundation for investigating sex differences in nervous systems across other species. However, Venkatachalam cautioned that results from worms cannot necessarily be applied directly to humans.“The goal is to learn principles of neuronal computation that are globally applicable,” he concluded to Northeastern news.

title: Plastic waste to become adsorbent for atmospheric water harvesting
content: Researchers have found that a way to give plastic waste a second life. Materials chemists from University of Vienna have found a way to convert several types of plastic waste into water-attracting polymer networks. These can take up water even in dry climates and release it again under moderate heating, e.g. using sunlight.The new effort offers a route to give plastic waste a second life as an adsorbent for atmospheric water harvesting.Discarded plastic packaging materials can be turned into useful productsUsing this method, discarded plastic packaging materials, old CDs, and even LEGO bricks can be transformed into materials that capture significant amounts of moisture from the air. Certain plastics comprise of aromatic polymers, whose molecular structures contain rings of six carbon molecules. These rings act as suitable sites from which to tie the polymer chains together, forming a porous network with tiny internal spaces. A subsequent treatment with sulfuric acid adds sulfonic acid groups that attract water even from relatively dry air, according to a press release. Researchers successfully produced such water-loving molecular sponges from various polystyrene packaging materials, old CDs made from polycarbonate, and LEGO bricks made of acrylonitrile butadiene styrene as feedstock. They also successfully treated a selected mixture of waste plastics, demonstrates versatility across these feedstocks, as per the release.Published in Chem Circularity, the findings establish a route from diverse aromatic plastic wastes to functional materials for atmospheric moisture capture. The ability to process a mixture suggests opportunities to reduce sorting requirements within compatible waste streams. Translation beyond the laboratory will require assessment of variable feedstocks, solvent and reagent recovery, production costs, and environmental impacts, alongside device integration and long-term durability. Addressing these questions will determine the scale at which this second life for waste plastics can contribute to circular materials management and water supply.Sponge made from general purpose polystyreneThe team revealed that the sponge made from general purpose polystyrene, the stuff single-use cutlery and CD cases are made from, could adsorb almost 60% of its own weight in water from humid air and even 20% in dry, desert-like conditions. The water can then be re-released for collection using mild heat sources, such as sunlight with most adsorption/desorption occuring within one hour. The sponges withstand the cycling process well, meaning they can be used to generate water over and over again.The team highlighted that the latest effort establishes a way to turn several aromatic waste plastics into effective materials for the generation of water from air, including mixed plastic feedstocks. Further work into assessing the long-term performance and overall resource requirements of the sponges is ongoing. “We demonstrate this approach using aromatic waste plastics from packaging, compact discs, and LEGO bricks. Hypercrosslinking and sulfonation transform these substrates into polymer networks for water capture, giving existing polymeric materials a second service life without first breaking them down into monomers,” said researchers in the study.

title: China urged to adopt US model to identify future military technology needs
content: A Chinese think tank has urged Beijing to adopt elements of a Pentagon initiative designed to identify the technologies that will shape future warfare, while avoiding potential conflicts of interest and weaknesses in the US assessment process. Project Meridian, launched in late September, aims to identify military capability gaps and guide investment in technologies including AI, autonomous systems, directed-energy weapons, robotics and biotechnology. In a recent analysis, the Beijing-based Blue Army Open-Source Intelligence Research Institute praised the initiative’s cross-sector approach and rapid assessment process, but questioned whether its short timetable and involvement of defense industry executives could undermine its conclusions.Project Meridian aims to identify future battlefield needsProject Meridian is intended to help the US Department of War assess how emerging technologies could change military operations and determine where investment is most urgently needed. The initiative is led by Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, and the MITRE Corporation, with Elon Musk, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey and former US House speaker Newt Gingrich serving as co-chairs.Its scope includes both established military domains and emerging areas such as space, cyber warfare, autonomous systems and directed energy. According to the Chinese think tank’s assessment, one of the project’s main strengths is its effort to connect operational requirements with technological development, rather than evaluating weapons systems in isolation.The report also highlighted the initiative’s planned 120-day assessment cycle and its use of analysts from different sectors. This approach reflects a broader challenge for the US military, which is that commercial technology often develops faster than traditional defense research, budgeting and procurement processes can accommodate.The think tank argued that China could benefit from adopting a similar model, bringing together military planners, research institutes, defense contractors, universities and civilian technology companies. Such cooperation could help identify capability gaps earlier and improve coordination between research funding and operational needs.Linking technology reviews to military deploymentThe Chinese analysis recommends an integrated system for assessing defense technologies, combining continuous monitoring of global developments with targeted reviews of specific military capability gaps. Rather than examining individual platforms separately, these assessments should also consider how well different systems work together, including data sharing, communications, interoperability and logistics.The report calls for each technology recommendation to identify the operational problem it is intended to solve, the capability gap involved, the maturity of the technology and the organization responsible for implementing it. Testing conditions and funding requirements should also be specified before a project advances, the report notes.A central recommendation is to establish a complete process connecting assessment to deployment. That would include project approval, prototyping, testing, validation by military units, large-scale deployment and subsequent review. The process should also account for changes to doctrine, training, personnel, organizational structures and logistical support.Despite praising Project Meridian’s approach, the Chinese report also warned that the participation of business leaders with existing defense industry interests could create conflicts of interest. Musk leads SpaceX, which holds major US government contracts, while Luckey co-founded Anduril Industries, a defense tech company developing autonomous systems and other military equipment.

title: Scientists Turn a Cancer-Fueling Protein Into a Powerful New Weapon Against Tumors
content:
A protein known for promoting cancer may hold an unexpected key to fighting it. New research reveals how manipulating immune cell metabolism could transform cancer treatment. Credit: Shutterstock
A protein that helps cancer grow could become an unlikely ally in treating it, with laboratory and mouse experiments showing that activating it in engineered immune cells curbs tumor growth.
Colorectal cancer has become the leading cause of cancer-related death in people under 50, and chemotherapy and newer immunotherapy drugs can fall short against its most common forms. That toll among younger people led researchers at
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL)
to investigate whether changing how immune cells burn fuel could help them fight the disease.
In a study published in
Nature Immunology
, the team found that activating a protein involved in fat burning helped engineered immune cells slow or stop tumor growth in laboratory and mouse experiments. The protein, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPARD), helps control how human cells use fat. The researchers activated it in CAR T cells, engineered immune cells already used in some cancer immunotherapies.
To test whether the altered CAR T cells could attack human colorectal cancer, the team used organoids, miniature tumors grown from patient tissue samples. They also tested the cells against human cancer cells in a dish and human cancer cells implanted in mice, finding that tumor growth slowed or stopped in each setting. The researchers also validated their findings in other tumor types, including breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and melanoma.
PPARD activation in the immune system increases the presence of tumor-infiltrating immune cells (green) in colorectal cancer, thereby suppressing tumor cells (blue and red) and slowing the cancer’s growth. Credit: Beyaz lab/CSHL
A cancer-promoting protein switches sides
PPARD is a transcription factor, a protein that helps control gene activity, and it usually promotes cancer growth. Investigating whether it could also help immune cells drew on a broader idea about fitness. Doctors have long recognized fitness as one of the strongest determinants of patient outcomes. For CSHL Assistant Professor Semir Beyaz, that concept extends beyond a patient’s physique to the capabilities of individual cells.
“We hypothesized that the fitness determinants of cancer and our immune cells may not be so different,” he said. “They’re in the same universe. They’re constrained by the same chemical and physical rules. So, it’s not surprising they’d end up evolving the same way.”
Before testing the approach in CAR T cells, Beyaz’s lab investigated PPARD in a mouse model of colorectal cancer. Although the cancer cells had their own PPARD, activating it in immune cells shifted the environment around the tumor from supporting cancer to opposing it. “It’s all about cell fitness,” Beyaz explains. “
What cells eat
affects who they are. When immune cells burn more fat, they become more fit for fighting cancer.”
Though used to treat blood cancers, CAR T cell therapy has had limited success against solid tumors. Activating PPARD in the immune cells could change that. Here, CAR T cells with (right) and without (left) PPARD activation are tested on colorectal cancer organoids. CAR T cells are shown in green, and organoids in red. How effective the different CAR T-cell groups are at killing off the organoids is measured in blue dye. Credit: Beyaz lab/CSHL
Beyaz likens PPARD’s opposing roles to “the force” from
Star Wars
. It can promote disease like Darth Vader carrying out the Emperor’s will, or turn against disease like Anakin Skywalker seeing the light. “It’s the classic fight between good and evil,” Beyaz says. “How can good ultimately prevail? Activating PPARD in immune cells could be the way.”
Testing immune fitness against endometriosis
The findings remain experimental, but Beyaz sees them as the “tip of the iceberg” for making cancer immunotherapy more effective. His lab is now applying the approach to endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory disease affecting one in 10 women for which more effective treatments are needed.
“Boosting immune cell fitness may also help with other conditions where the immune system fails to clear diseased cells,” Beyaz says.

K. Westcott, Samuel E. Weinberg, Saar I. Gill, Nathalie Y. R. Agar and Semir Beyaz, 14 October 2026,

title: New Triple-Action Drug Helps People With Diabetes Lose Up to 15% of Their Body Weight
content:
Retatrutide is an experimental once-weekly injectable drug being developed to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity. Unlike existing medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, it targets three hormone receptors involved in blood sugar regulation, appetite, and metabolism: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. Credit: Shutterstock
An experimental drug that targets three metabolic pathways has shown promising results in people with type 2 diabetes.
An experimental drug that targets three metabolic pathways has produced substantial improvements in blood sugar control and weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes. In a phase 3 clinical trial published in
The Lancet
, participants receiving the once-weekly injection lost an average of up to 15.3% of their body weight over 40 weeks, alongside significant reductions in long-term blood sugar levels.
The drug, called retatrutide, belongs to an emerging generation of treatments designed to influence several hormones involved in metabolism. Unlike existing medications that activate one or two hormone receptors, retatrutide acts on three, potentially offering a different approach to treating diabetes and obesity.
Significant Improvements in Blood Sugar and Weight
The trial found that retatrutide reduced HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar over approximately three months, by 1.69 to 1.94 percentage points, depending on the dose. Participants receiving a placebo experienced a smaller reduction of 0.81 percentage points.
Weight loss also increased with the dose. Participants receiving 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg of retatrutide lost an average of 11.5%, 13.9%, and 15.3% of their body weight, respectively. Those given a placebo lost an average of 2.6%.
How Retatrutide Differs From Ozempic and Mounjaro
Retatrutide activates three hormone receptors involved in regulating blood sugar, appetite, and energy metabolism: GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon. By comparison, Ozempic targets GLP-1, while Mounjaro activates both GLP-1 and GIP.
The addition of glucagon receptor activity could help explain retatrutide’s effects on body weight. Although glucagon normally helps raise blood sugar, it also influences how the body uses and expends energy. Combining its activity with GLP-1 and GIP signaling may support weight loss while maintaining improved glucose control. However, the trial did not directly establish how much each pathway contributed to the observed benefits.
Promising Results, but Longer-Term Safety Remains Under Study
Researchers conducted the 40-week trial at 48 sites across the United States, Mexico, and India. Of 930 adults screened, 537 were randomly assigned to receive one of three retatrutide doses or a placebo. All participants had type 2 diabetes that was inadequately controlled through diet and exercise alone and were not taking diabetes medications.
The most common side effects were gastrointestinal problems, generally mild to moderate, that tended to improve over time. Between 2% and 5% of participants receiving retatrutide discontinued treatment because of adverse events. No severe hypoglycemia was reported. Two participants died during the study, but both deaths were assessed as unrelated to the treatment.
Although the results support retatrutide’s potential as a diabetes treatment, the study did not compare it directly with currently available drugs such as Ozempic or Mounjaro. Additional clinical trials and longer-term follow-up are needed to determine whether its benefits persist and to better establish its safety profile.
Reference: “Efficacy and safety of retatrutide, a GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptor agonist, in people with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control with diet and exercise (TRANSCEND-T2D-1): a double-blind, randomised, phase 3 trial” by Harpreet S Bajaj, Michelle Welch, Parag Shah, Eduardo Luna, Fatima-Zahra Jaouimaa, Bing Liu, Rong Liu, Yanyun Chen, Hiren Patel and Amy Bartee, 6 June 2026,
The Lancet

title: Not Getting Enough Daylight Could Be Linked to a Higher Risk of Dementia
content:
Most people spend much of their day indoors, where lighting is typically far dimmer than natural daylight. Researchers are examining whether these differences in everyday light exposure have implications for long-term brain health. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers found that insufficient exposure to bright daytime light may be a stronger predictor of dementia than several established risk factors.
Greater exposure to bright light during the day may be associated with a lower risk of developing dementia, according to research involving nearly 88,000 adults. Participants whose average daytime light exposure exceeded 1,000 lux had a 16% lower dementia risk than those exposed to dimmer conditions.
The study, published in
General Psychiatry
, analyzed light exposure in 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with light sensors for seven days. Over a median follow-up of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia. The association between brighter daytime light and lower dementia risk remained significant after researchers accounted for numerous health, lifestyle, and environmental factors.
How Much Daytime Light Is Associated With Lower Dementia Risk?
Both light intensity and exposure duration were associated with dementia risk. Participants who experienced at least 42 minutes of bright daytime light at 5,000 lux or higher had a 17% lower risk than those with less exposure. For comparison, 1,000 lux is roughly equivalent to the brightness of an overcast day outdoors, considerably brighter than typical indoor lighting.
In a separate analysis, receiving fewer than 42 minutes of bright daytime light ranked as a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors, including obesity, alcohol consumption, and traumatic brain injury. By contrast, nighttime light exposure showed no statistically significant association with dementia risk.
Why Light Exposure May Matter for Brain Health
Daytime light helps regulate circadian rhythms, the body’s internal timing system that influences sleep, daily activity, and cognitive function. Additional analyses suggested that differences in these rhythms and certain brain structures might partly explain the relationship. The association was particularly pronounced among evening chronotypes, people carrying the APOE ε4 genetic variant, and those exposed to higher levels of nighttime light.
However, the observational findings do not establish that increasing daytime light exposure prevents dementia. Light exposure was measured for only one week, and wrist sensors cannot precisely capture the amount of light reaching the eyes. Further research is needed to determine whether changing light exposure can directly influence dementia risk.
“Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk,” said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.

title: Researchers Unleash Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes in Just 300 Attoseconds
content:
In an undulator with permanent magnets of alternating polarisation, a wiggling cloud of electrons emits a sharp, short pulse of X-rays. Credit: European XFEL/Tobias Wüstefeld
Researchers used the European XFEL to produce ultrashort X-ray flashes that reached record intensity for this type of pulse.
To understand chemical reactions and perhaps one day control the electrons involved, scientists need a detailed picture of how electrons behave inside atoms and molecules. X-rays offer a way to probe that behavior, but the flashes can also change the sample they are meant to examine. Researchers therefore need enough light to gather useful information before those changes become substantial.
At the European XFEL, a team has now concentrated X-ray flashes onto an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair. The pulses lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds, with each attosecond equal to a billionth of a billionth of a second.
The experiment used hard X-rays, light with particularly short wavelengths, and took place in April 2026 at the facility’s MID instrument. The results are published in
Focusing ultrashort X-rays to extreme intensity
“A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL,” says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. “But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter.”
To concentrate that energy, the researchers used an advanced Kirkpatrick–Baez, or AKB, optical system brought from Japan. Each flash underwent four reflections in total, with one of the system’s two extremely precise mirrors focusing the light vertically and the other horizontally. Together, they concentrated the X-rays into a spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers. A nanometer is a billionth of a meter.
Copper atoms amplify the X-ray signal
To test that calculation, the researchers shone the pulses onto copper foil. The X-rays knocked electrons out of deep inner shells within the copper atoms, leaving gaps that other electrons could fill. As electrons moved into those gaps, they released X-ray light. At sufficiently high intensities, that light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to emit additional X-rays in the same direction, amplifying the signal through a process called amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.
“It is almost magical to see this happening,” says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument. “Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction.”
The ASE signal initially rose rapidly as the pulse energy increased, then leveled off at higher energies. This saturation, expected only at extremely high X-ray intensities, provided independent confirmation of the team’s calculation.
European XFEL expects to receive its own AKB system in early 2027. Once installed and commissioned, the system is intended to give researchers from around the world using the MID instrument access to similarly brief, intense X-ray flashes.
Reference: “Generation of high-fluence and high-intensity hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL” by 19 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.613284

title: NASA’s James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Alien Planet That’s Not Quite Round
content:
WASP-17b’s atmosphere is shaped by powerful equatorial winds carrying heat from its permanent dayside to its nightside. The evening side (left) is hotter and more extended, while the morning side (right) is cooler. Using transmission strings, researchers mapped the atmosphere’s uneven shape for the first time. Credit: Engine House and Hannah Wakeford.
Weather maps of distant planets are a step closer after the James Webb Space Telescope distinguished hotter and cooler regions around the giant exoplanet WASP-17b.
One side of WASP-17b’s atmosphere extends farther into space than the other, giving this intensely hot giant planet an uneven outline. Astronomers have now mapped that distortion with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), finding a pattern consistent with predictions of how heat and powerful winds shape a world with permanent day and night sides.
WASP-17b is a hot Jupiter, a giant planet that orbits close to its star, about 1,300 light-years from Earth. The study, co-led by
Cornell University
in the United States and the
University of Bristol
in the United Kingdom, was published in
Nature Astronomy
. It marks the first application of a method called transmission strings, developed at Bristol by astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford.
“Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds,” said Wakeford, a study co-author and associate professor of astrophysics at the University of Bristol.
Resolving differences around the atmospheric edge
JWST, the largest telescope in space, has already enabled researchers to use a technique called eclipse mapping, which measures changes in light as a planet passes behind its host star. Transmission strings, also called transit mapping, follows the planet as it crosses in front of the star. It analyzes the light passing through different parts of the atmosphere’s edge, or limb, to distinguish conditions around that boundary. Traditional modeling instead extracts a single spectrum, a measurement of light across different wavelengths, averaged over the entire limb.
Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell, began the investigation at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics.
JWST observations reveal WASP-17b’s uneven atmosphere as it crosses its star. Hot gas expands the red evening side, while cooler gas contracts the blue morning side. This technique could help scientists map weather patterns on distant planets. Credit: Engine House and Hannah Wakeford.
“Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet,” Alderson said. “We’re able to go around the edge. So, we’ve gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak.”
Heat swells the evening atmosphere
On WASP-17b, the mapped bulge lies on the evening side of the equator. There, jets of wind carry heat from the permanently illuminated day side toward the permanently shadowed night side, inflating the atmosphere relative to the equator’s cooler morning side. The location matches what theory and previous modeling had indicated.
“Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend – pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be,” Alderson said.
The study’s findings on atmospheric chemical composition and temperature differences, both from equator to poles and between the day and night sides, also agree with theoretical predictions and other modeling techniques.
“Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting,” Wakeford said.
Toward weather maps of distant planets
Together, the findings provide one of the most comprehensive three-dimensional views of an exoplanet’s atmosphere. They also establish a benchmark for comparison with the more than 6,000 other exoplanets confirmed to date.
“This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter,” Alderson said.
The successful demonstration on WASP-17b opens the way to applying transmission strings to many more planets. The method is beginning to distinguish conditions across different latitudes, extending atmospheric maps beyond the contrast between day and night. That is a first step toward mapping weather-scale patterns in exoplanet climates.
Reference: “A spatial map of the atmospheric limb of a hot Jupiter” by Lili Alderson, Hannah R. Wakeford, David Grant, Nikole K. Lewis, Avinash Verma, Jayesh Goyal, Mark Hammond, Daniel Valentine, Natalie H. Allen, Ana Glidden, Amélie Gressier, Jingcheng Huang, Maura Lally, Dana R. title: What Kills Schrödinger’s Cat? Scientists Just Ruled Out a 60-Year-Old Theory
content:
Schrödinger’s cat illustrates the quantum paradox of an object existing in two states at once. A new study tests whether gravity could explain why such quantum behavior disappears in the everyday world. Credit: FQxI/Gabriel Fitzpatrick (2026)
Gravity has been proposed as a reason quantum superpositions become difficult to observe in everyday objects. A new experiment challenges one longstanding model of this process.
A detector buried deep beneath an Italian mountain has challenged a decades-old theory about why quantum behavior disappears from the world we experience. After 62 days of measurements, researchers found no trace of the faint radiation predicted by a model in which gravity disrupts quantum states. The result rules out this particular explanation while leaving open the possibility that gravity contributes to quantum decoherence.
Decoherence helps explain why particles can display unusual quantum behavior, such as existing in superpositions of different states, while everyday objects appear to follow classical physics. “One of the deepest questions in modern physics is why the strange quantum behavior that governs atoms and elementary particles seems to disappear in the macroscopic world we experience every day,” says Catalina Curceanu, director of research and spokesperson for the VIP Collaboration at the National Laboratory of Frascati of the National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN-LNF) in Italy.
Could Fluctuations in Spacetime Disrupt Quantum Behavior?
In the 1960s, Hungarian physicist Frigyes Károlyházy proposed that spacetime undergoes constant, extremely small fluctuations. According to his model, these disturbances gradually destroy quantum superpositions, preventing large objects from displaying effects such as those illustrated by Schrödinger’s famous thought experiment involving a cat that is both alive and dead.
The proposal connects quantum mechanics with Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Although Károlyházy’s original idea dates back decades, it has continued to attract attention. FQxI researcher Angelo Bassi and his colleagues recently
reformulated the model
, allowing its predictions to be examined experimentally.
The hypothesized fluctuations cannot be measured directly, but they should have a detectable consequence. They would cause electrically charged particles to undergo tiny random accelerations, producing extremely weak electromagnetic radiation. Detecting that radiation, or establishing its absence, provides a way to test the theory.
Searching for a Faint Signal Deep Underground
The FQxI-funded experiment took place at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory (INFN-LNGS), the world’s largest underground laboratory dedicated to fundamental physics research. Located beneath 1.4 kilometers (0.87 miles) of rock, the facility is shielded from much of the cosmic radiation that could otherwise overwhelm such a weak signal.
“The natural shielding provided by the rock creates one of the quietest environments on Earth for detecting extremely rare physical phenomena,” says Curceanu.
The researchers used a high-purity germanium crystal roughly the size of a coffee mug, enclosed within layers of copper and lead shielding. After collecting measurements for 62 days, they accounted for the expected background radiation and searched the remaining data for the signature predicted by Károlyházy’s model. They found no matching signal. The findings were published in the
New Journal of Physics
What the Missing Radiation Means for Gravity
“This absence of a signal is itself a major scientific result,” says Curceanu. The measurements exclude the tested version of Károlyházy’s model, placing new constraints on explanations that attribute quantum decoherence to fluctuations in spacetime.
The findings do not establish that gravity has no role in decoherence. Other gravitational mechanisms remain possible, and the broader relationship between quantum mechanics and general relativity is unresolved. “By ruling out one of the oldest and most natural gravity-induced decoherence models, this work narrows the search for the theory describing the interplay between gravity and quantum mechanics, bringing us one step closer to understanding one of the deepest mysteries in fundamental physics,” says Curceanu.
Bringing Quantum Gravity Within Experimental Reach
Károlyházy’s proposal is based on the idea that nature imposes a fundamental limit on how precisely distances and positions can be measured. Related concepts appear in modern efforts to reconcile gravity with quantum mechanics, including string theory and loop quantum gravity. In these approaches, the familiar picture of perfectly measurable spacetime may break down at extremely small scales.
“Every quantum gravity approach ends up with predicting the existence of a minimal length connected to the uncertainty in the measurement of spacetime,” says Kristian Piscicchia, a quantum physicist at the Enrico Fermi Research Center/INFN/VIP in Italy and the experimental lead on the study. The new measurements do not establish whether such a minimum length exists, but they constrain one proposed physical consequence of spacetime uncertainty.
“Precision experiments are now reaching a level of sensitivity where they can test ideas that, until recently, belonged almost exclusively to the realm of theoretical speculation,” says Curceanu. “As sensitivity improves, the boundary between theory and measurement continues to move, opening new possibilities for discovering the fundamental principles that govern our universe.”
Reference: “Experimental exclusion of a generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model” by Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola and Catalina Curceanu, 19 June 2026,
New Journal of Physics
DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/ae774c
The research was supported by the Foundational Questions Institute, FQxI, through the Consciousness in the Physical World program.

title: Quantum Computing Breakthrough Opens a New Path to Larger, More Powerful Processors
content:
Technology
Silicon-based quantum computers could benefit from a breakthrough in controlling multiple qubits without sacrificing precision. Credit: Stock
Keeping silicon quantum bits accurate while they work together could help turn established chipmaking technology into larger quantum computers capable of tackling increasingly complex problems.
The manufacturing technology behind everyday computer chips could help build larger quantum computers. Silicon spin qubits offer that possibility, but the precision they achieve on their own can slip when several are controlled at once.
Researchers from the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now demonstrated a way to preserve much of that precision during simultaneous operation. Working with five silicon qubits controlled through a single shared microwave line, they identified a major source of control errors and developed a calibration protocol to compensate for it. Their study was published in
Nature Physics
Quantum bits, or qubits, represent combinations of the conventional binary states 0 and 1. In silicon spin qubits, information is encoded in the spin of an electron trapped in a silicon substrate. Microwave signals manipulate those spins to carry out quantum operations. A useful quantum computer must perform many such operations simultaneously, making reliable parallel control essential.
High precision with three qubits at once
The team’s optimized device design and carefully calibrated microwave pulses produced single-qubit gate fidelities well above 99.99% on each of the five qubits when tested individually, with the best approaching 99.999%. Fidelity measures how accurately a quantum operation is performed. With the new protocol, fidelities stayed above 99.99% when up to three qubits operated at the same time.
“This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors,” says Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments.
Rendered illustration of five silicon spin qubits controlled in parallel through a shared microwave line. Credit: RIKEN
When all five qubits operated simultaneously, fidelities remained at approximately 99.9%, close to the practical requirements of fault-tolerant quantum computing, which is designed to keep computations reliable despite errors.
“Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal,” says Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST’s Moonshot Goal 6.
Correcting phase shifts, pair by pair
The researchers traced a major source of the accuracy loss during parallel operation to the AC Stark shift, an effect induced by the microwave control signals. It changes a qubit’s effective energy levels and shifts the phase of its quantum state. Phase describes how the wave-like components of that state line up with one another. These unwanted shifts interfere with the control needed to perform the intended operation.
Correcting those shifts required a calibration method that could accommodate more qubits without separately testing every possible combination. Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author, who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research, explains how the team approached that challenge. “Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts.”
“By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration,” says Camenzind, “our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon’s compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.”
The remaining loss of accuracy was attributed to drive-induced decoherence caused by the increased microwave power needed for simultaneous operation. This involves a loss of quantum coherence, distinct from the phase shifts addressed by the calibration protocol. “This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error,” says Camenzind.
Reference: “Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array” by Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan and Seigo Tarucha, 15 October 2026,
Nature Physics
DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2

title: Scientists Discover Metals That Refuse To Crack at an Astonishing -424°F
content:
Technology
Electron microscopy image showing new defects forming between neighbouring crystals of the niobium-titanium-based alloys. Scale bar: 40 μm. Credit: Crook et al. 2026
Two experimental alloys resisted cracking at −424°F by forming new crystal defects, offering a possible route to tougher metals for extreme cold.
Most metals become stronger as they cool, but some also become more vulnerable to breaking. Iron, tungsten, and chromium belong to a class called body-centered cubic metals, whose atomic arrangement can make them increasingly brittle as temperatures fall. A crack that the metal might otherwise accommodate by bending or stretching can instead cause a fracture.
That ability to deform depends heavily on the movement of dislocations, line-like defects in the metal’s crystal structure. At low temperatures, these defects become harder to move, limiting how much the material can deform to relieve the forces building up around a crack.
Alloys resist cracking at −424°F
Two experimental niobium-titanium-based alloys avoided this problem even at 20 kelvin, about −253°C (−424°F), by changing how they deform. An international team led by the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford found that the alloys remained remarkably resistant to cracking, with no measurable transition to brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested. Their findings, published in
, reveal how the alloys create new opportunities for deformation when the usual mechanism becomes difficult.
Experimental setup of the cryogenic mechanical testing rig at the EnginX beamline at the ISIS Muon and Neutron Source. Credit: Dong Liu
To test the alloys under these conditions, the researchers used the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire. They cooled samples with gaseous helium to around −253°C, then exposed them to a neutron beam while a testing machine pulled them from both ends. The tests precisely measured how much force the samples could withstand and how far they stretched before breaking.
Crystal defects that keep alloys deforming
Electron microscopes allowed the team to examine structural changes around cracks and inside the tested metal. The researchers observed nanoscale twinning, a process in which tiny regions of the crystal reorganize into mirror-image orientations, coupled with a local transformation of the crystal structure. They also used atom-probe analysis to map the distribution of individual elements and computer modeling to investigate how the different mechanisms worked together to prevent brittle failure.
When the newly formed structures reached boundaries between neighboring crystals, they created concentrated points of stress that triggered new dislocations. These fresh defects allowed the material to keep deforming and absorb the forces around a crack. Even as existing dislocations became harder to move, the alloys could generate new ones at these boundaries.
The Engin-X beamline. Credit: STFC
Lead author Dr. David Cook, who was at the University of California, Berkeley, during the study and is now at the University of Cambridge, said: “Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures.”
Potential applications include components exposed to exceptionally cold conditions in the energy, transportation, and aerospace sectors.
ISIS Neutron and Muon source. Credit: STFC
Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu, of the University of Oxford’s Department of Engineering Science, said: “For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application.”
Reference: “Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K” by David H. Cook, Xiaoyu Chen, Michael O’Leary, Satish Rao, Wenqing Wang, Calvin H. Belcher, Madelyn Payne, Pedro Borges, Tung Lik Lee, Arun Devaraj, Mark Asta, Enrique J. Lavernia, Diran Apelian, Andrew M. Minor, Dong Liu, Punit Kumar and Robert O. Ritchie, 14 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11065-7
The research was principally supported by the US Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, Materials Sciences and Engineering Division, through the Damage-Tolerance in Structural Materials program (KC-13) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) under contract DE-AC02-CH11231.

title: Chernobyl’s Radioactive Debris Is Defying Scientists’ Expectations 40 Years Later
content:
Chemistry
The Chernobyl disaster occurred on April 26, 1986, when a reactor at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Soviet Ukraine exploded during a failed safety test. The accident released massive amounts of radioactive material into the atmosphere, contaminating large areas of Europe and forcing thousands of people to evacuate. Credit: Shutterstock
Some of Chernobyl’s radioactive debris is more resilient than scientists expected, offering clues to when the material trapped inside could escape into the environment.
Radioactive dust still contaminates the soil around Chernobyl four decades after explosions scattered debris from the nuclear reactor in Ukraine in 1986. The fragments measure just 8 to 50 micrometers across and remain highly radioactive. Assessing their risks requires understanding how quickly they break down and release radioactive substances, yet scientists still cannot fully explain why these “hot particles” weather at different rates.
An analysis of six fragments by researchers at Leibniz University Hannover and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) found that the nuclear fuel’s crystal structure has remained largely intact. The examined particles are chemically more stable than previously assumed, retaining fission products, substances created when atomic nuclei split. That could limit the release of radioactive material into surrounding soil and water, while helping researchers refine assessments of the risks these particles pose.
2,000 angles reveal each particle’s structure
Examining the fragments required complex synchrotron X-ray diffraction experiments, which reveal a material’s internal structure through the way it scatters X-rays. HZDR researcher and crystallographer Dr. Christoph Hennig carried out the first successful structural investigation of this kind at the Rossendorf Beamline in Grenoble, working with Tobias Weissenborn, a physicist and doctoral candidate at Leibniz University Hannover.
“The colleagues from Hanover and I used various methods to isolate the particles from Ukrainian soil samples and attach them to tungsten electrodes,” Weissenborn explains. The team secured the samples within several confinement layers before shipping them to Grenoble for examination by Hennig’s team.
Hot particle from the 1986 reactor accident: The nuclear fuel particle is partially fused with zirconium oxide. Credit: Laura Stalmann
“First, we had to figure out how to examine the particle structure,” Hennig explains. “Ultimately, we fully rotated the particles in an X-ray beam focused down to 100 micrometers—about the thickness of a human hair. We measured each particle from 2,000 different angles to seamlessly capture all the reflections.”
Those measurements allowed the researchers to identify different oxide phases, or distinct crystalline forms, within the samples. This phase analysis can help estimate how quickly the fragments release radioactive substances as they deteriorate and form different uranium oxides.
Heat and fire reshaped the fuel
The particles’ structures reflect the different conditions the fuel experienced during the disaster. “There are three classes of these particles,” Weissenborn explains. “First, there are particles that are chemically and physically still very similar to the nuclear fuel uranium dioxide. Then, there are particles that are partially or fully encased in, or completely fused with, their zirconium layer.”
Particles containing fused fuel and zirconium formed when temperatures inside the reactor rose dramatically. The heat melted the fuel and bonded it to its surrounding protective layer of zirconium, a highly resistant metal.
“The third type of particle was created when the graphite-moderator caught fire,” Weissenborn adds. The graphite normally slowed fast neutrons to help sustain the nuclear chain reaction. During the accident, it burned for ten days.
“In the process, the fuel oxidized into various uranium oxides,” Weissenborn explains. These included U₃O₈, a mechanically unstable compound that readily breaks into microscopic particles that wind can carry away. Inhaling such radioactive dust poses severe health risks. Protective suits are still required to enter the affected areas.
Six particles cannot establish regional safety
The stability observed in the six examined fragments cannot yet be assumed to extend across the contaminated region. “However, every single particle has a different structure,” warns Weissenborn, “and our experiment only studied six such particles from two different locations.” Establishing broader patterns would require examining many more particles collected from far more locations.
“And even if we obtained some averages at some point, we still wouldn’t be able to make universal statements about health risks in the region,” Weissenborn cautions. “Because even if the particles decay in a largely uniform pattern, there will always be outliers, more persistent particles, that will release radionuclides at a later point in time.”
The findings therefore offer no basis for lifting restrictions on the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone anytime soon. Weissenborn and Hennig are already conducting follow-up experiments on the debris’s highly radioactive transuranic phases, which contain elements with atomic numbers higher than uranium’s.
Reference: “X-ray diffraction phase analysis of single hot particles from Chornobyl” by Tobias Weissenborn, Christoph Hennig, Laura Leifermann, Paul Hanemann, Eleanor Lawrence Bright, Florian Meurer, Aaron Lehnert, Kristina Kvashnina and Clemens Walther, 18 February 2026,
Journal of Hazardous Materials
DOI: 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141533

title: The World May Be Much Closer to a Major Conservation Goal Than Scientists Thought
content:
A new study suggests that global land conservation may be much closer to an important international target than official figures indicate. Credit: Shutterstock
The world may be closer to its 30% land conservation goal, but gaps in grassland and shrubland protection show why acreage alone cannot safeguard wildlife.
Some areas that support wildlife appear in national conservation records but are missing from the global tally. Including them could bring the share of land in some form of conservation to 26.8%, or nearly 27%, well above the officially reported 18.5%.
That difference changes the picture for an international commitment to protect nature. Almost every country has agreed to conserve 30% of land and sea by 2030 to help halt and reverse the biodiversity crisis, yet official figures suggest that progress on land has stalled.
“With four years to go, the terrestrial component of the 30% target seems out of reach. Our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” says lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral research associate at the Institute of Zoology in London.
Conservation areas beyond the official count
To build the broader estimate, an international team of conservation experts combined global measures of protection with national data on conservation areas. The study, published in
, was led by the Durrell Institute of Conservation and Ecology at the University of Kent in the United Kingdom.
“We need much more effort to officially recognize the existing conservation areas that are currently only recorded in national datasets.” That is the call from the study’s lead investigator, Bob Smith, director of the Durrell Institute of Conservation and Ecology at the University of Kent in Canterbury. The university is part of the London and Southeast University Group.
Grasslands and shrublands need more protection
Grasslands and shrublands, home to uniquely adapted wildlife, still have limited protection even within this larger conservation network. These gaps mean that expanding the total area alone cannot ensure that the full range of habitats receives protection.
Co-author Heather Bingham, who leads the Protected Planet Initiative at the United Nations Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre in Cambridge, stresses that “conserving 30% of lands and seas is not sufficient on its own. The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact for biodiversity.”
Meeting those requirements means connecting conservation areas, including diverse ecosystems, and managing sites fairly for local people. Smith adds, “We also need to focus much more on improving the effectiveness of all conservation areas, as increasing the area of land under conservation will do little unless these sites are effectively and fairly managed.”

title: A 1,000-Year-Old DNA Mystery Links Hawaii and Easter Island and Reveals Hidden Genetic Dangers
content:
Easter Island, also known as Rapa Nui, is a remote island in the southeastern Pacific Ocean, famous for its enormous stone statues called moai. Located thousands of miles from Hawaii, the island was settled by ancient Polynesian voyagers whose remarkable seafaring abilities continue to intrigue scientists. Credit: Shutterstock
The DNA that traces Hawaii’s settlement also points to overlooked disease risks, with some globally rare variants common enough among Eastern Polynesians to warrant screening.
Hawaii and Easter Island lie about 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) apart, roughly the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru. New genetic evidence suggests that ancient sailors from the Easter Island region crossed that vast stretch of the Pacific to settle Hawaii. No written record describes their journey, but traces of it remain in the DNA of people living on the islands today.
Stanford Medicine researchers and collaborators uncovered the connection by analyzing genomes from more than 1,000 people throughout Polynesia. Their study, published Oct. 8 in
, extends a settlement route that researchers previously thought had ended at Easter Island.
“What we uncover in this paper is where the native people of Hawaii had come from,” said Alexander Ioannidis, PhD, assistant professor of genetics and of biomedical data science at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study. “Hawaii is the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere, so it’s a long way from everything.”
The study’s other co-senior author is Keolu Fox, PhD, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of California, San Diego, and a Native Hawaiian.
Hawaii’s ancestry points toward Easter Island
Across Polynesia, more than 1,000 islands occupy an expanse of ocean roughly equal to the combined areas of North and South America. Reconstructing connections among those islands, from tropical Hawaii to temperate Easter Island in the far South Pacific, requires evidence that can reach back through centuries of migration.
“People on the islands today have encoded in their genomes essentially the genealogy of all of their ancestors,” Ioannidis said.
To follow that ancestry, the researchers isolated genome segments of Polynesian origin, excluding more recent contributions from populations such as Europeans and Asians. They then compared stretches of DNA shared by people from different islands. These stretches, called identity-by-descent segments, come from a common ancestor. Longer shared segments generally indicate that two people shared an ancestor more recently.
Alexander Ioannidis on Easter Island. Credit: Stanford Medicine
Among the populations compared, Native Hawaiians shared the most Polynesian ancestry with people on Easter Island, followed by people on Mangareva, nearly 3,000 kilometers (1,860 miles) from Easter Island. Ioannidis interprets that pattern as consistent with a culture capable of exceptionally long voyages. Seafarers who could reach Easter Island from Mangareva would also have had the capabilities needed to travel onward to Hawaii.
Double-hulled catamarans carried provisions such as taro, sweet potatoes, and bananas, which could supply food for weeks at sea and crops for a new settlement. An
earlier study
The team’s
previous genetic reconstruction
had traced Polynesian settlement from Samoa to Fiji and Tonga, then gradually eastward through the Cook Islands, the Society Islands, which include Tahiti, and Mangareva. It placed settlement of Easter Island around 1210. The new findings suggest that this was another stop along an expanding migration route.
Tahiti’s founding generation estimated at 800
Genetic evidence also allowed the researchers to investigate how many people founded an island population and what happened afterward. Tahiti offered the largest collection of genomes in their dataset, making it the focus of a more detailed analysis. By comparing identity-by-descent segments among people from the island, the team estimated that its founding generation consisted of approximately 800 people who arrived about 34 generations ago, around 1070.
That estimate covers a single generation of people of reproductive age. It does not include children or elders who may have accompanied them.
“Archaeologists and others have long wondered how many people founded these islands. That’s not something that you can determine definitively from archaeology, but we can determine it from genetics,” Ioannidis said.
The analysis reconstructed rapid population growth on Tahiti after settlement, followed by a substantial population crash in the 1700s after European colonial contact. Similar reconstructions are underway for Easter Island and Hawaii, but they will require additional genomes.
Island settlements narrowed the gene pool
Each island settlement also shaped the genetic inheritance of later generations. When a small group separates from a larger population to establish a new one, it carries only part of the original population’s genetic diversity. This bottleneck, known as a founder effect, can make an otherwise rare variant more common among descendants, including variants associated with disease. Across Polynesia, small groups, perhaps only a few hundred people at a time, founded successive island populations over several centuries.
“We thought Easter Island was the end when we were first doing that study, but now it looks like it was part of this path to Hawaii, which is really incredible,” Ioannidis said. “By the time you’ve gotten all the way to Hawaii, you’re at the end of a series of founder effects, so it’s really intense.”
Founder effects have been extensively studied in populations of European descent, including the Amish, Ashkenazi Jews, and Finns. That research has led to standard screening for certain inherited conditions. The new analysis indicates that the scale of these effects among Eastern Polynesians has been overlooked.
“What we discovered is in the Eastern Polynesians, such as Native Hawaiians, the founder effects are more than an order of magnitude, so more than 10 times, larger than what we have in the populations of European descent we’ve studied so well,” Ioannidis said.
Disease variants common enough for screening
To examine the medical implications, the researchers analyzed three genetic variants recently linked to autosomal recessive conditions among Eastern Polynesians. These conditions generally develop when a person inherits a disease-causing version of the relevant gene from each parent. The variants occur in
ADAMTSL4
, associated with dislocation of the eye’s lens,
, associated with progressive vision loss, and
, associated with kidney failure.
Although these variants are exceedingly rare worldwide and barely represented in international genome databases, the researchers found carrier rates of 2% to 3% among the Eastern Polynesians studied. Those rates meet standard thresholds for recommending genetic screening. Larger genomic studies could identify additional clinically relevant variants that are unusually common in Polynesian populations and help guide precision medicine.
“We should be doing more sequencing and trying to characterize more of these conditions among Native Hawaiians,” said Ioannidis, noting that the Native Hawaiian population is nearly twice the size of the Amish population. “We don’t have recommendations for genetic testing, and there’s no reimbursement from insurance because these are conditions we don’t even know about.”
“This is a population that should be getting research resources and attention from geneticists even more urgently.”
Reference: “Message in a bottleneck: Nested founder effects from French Polynesia to Rapa Nui and Hawaiʻi” by Cole Shanks, Edward C. Huang, Christophe Thomassin, Anne-Katrin Emde, Vahinetua Rodière, Mauricio Moraga, Karla Sandoval, Tony Merriman, Tristan Pascart, Andrés Moreno-Estrada, Stephane E. Castel, Keolu Fox and Alexander G. Ioannidis, 8 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.aec7662
