title: Something Unexpected Is Happening to Antarctica’s Collapsing Ice Cliffs
content:
Antarctica’s towering ice cliffs may be more resilient than scientists once feared. New satellite observations reveal surprising natural mechanisms that could reshape predictions of future sea level rise. Credit: Shutterstock
Satellite observations show Antarctic ice cliffs stabilizing after unexpectedly rapid collapse, challenging assumptions about runaway ice loss and its contribution to rising seas.
Antarctica’s ice shelves help hold back the ice sheet behind them, but rising temperatures are causing these supports to melt and break apart at record rates. As sheer ice cliffs are left exposed, scientists have worried that a collapse could reveal a taller cliff farther inland, setting off a chain of failures that eats into the ice sheet and raises seas worldwide.
In a four-year satellite survey of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs, researchers at MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) found that the tallest cliffs they examined closely did collapse, and the ice sheet in those regions retreated faster than models predicted. “But that retreat was short-lived,” says Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program.
Needell conducted the study, published in
, with Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.
Rapid collapse without runaway retreat
The observations came from NASA’s Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2), which passes over Earth’s polar regions. Its laser altimeter measures the height of ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica. The team analyzed measurements collected every three months from 2019 to 2023 to determine how tall the cliffs were and how they changed over time.
Those measurements offered a much broader test of a proposed process called marine ice cliff instability, or MICI. In this scenario, a cliff exceeding a critical height collapses under its own weight. If that exposes a taller cliff, the failures continue inland. Previous studies had investigated this process by modeling ice’s physical properties, scaling those relationships up to entire cliffs, and combining the predictions with a few observations from Antarctica.
Researchers at MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) analyzed over 15,000 ice cliffs in Antarctica to reveal how they behave over time. Credit: Caroline Needell
“Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height,” Needell notes. “That’s the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat.”
Across the satellite survey, the average ice cliff stood about 30 meters (98 feet) tall, well below that proposed threshold. A few rare cliffs exceeded 100 meters (328 feet), roughly the height of the Statue of Liberty, giving the researchers an opportunity to examine what happened near and above the predicted danger point.
“After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let’s zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they’re behaving,” Needell says.
The team focused on four cliffs in four regions around the Antarctic ice sheet. These cliffs were roughly 100 meters tall, with the tallest reaching 127 meters (417 feet). Tracking them through the same four years of measurements revealed that their rapid collapse and retreat did not continue unchecked. The ice eventually spread back out toward the ocean.
“It’s this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization,” Needell says. “That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height.”
Rising ground can stabilize ice cliffs
The researchers first examined the shape of the land beneath the ice. Over relatively flat ground, changes in the ice surface’s elevation reflect changes in the thickness of the ice itself. Where the ground rises, however, some of that elevation comes from the land underneath, leaving a thinner layer of ice above it. Such a rise could act as a speed bump for retreat by making the overlying ice less prone to collapse. When the team checked Antarctic topographic measurements, they found that cliffs stabilized around places where the underlying land rose.
Taller cliffs also “thin out” faster, the researchers found. As they collapse, they settle into shorter, more stable cliffs, limiting further collapse.
“Now we know what to look for,” Needell says. “We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise.”
Support from broken ice and seawater
Conditions in front of the cliffs offered additional clues. In the broader survey, cliffs that stayed roughly in place had thicker mélange, the slushy mixture of broken icebergs and sea ice that collects against a cliff’s ocean-facing edge.
“We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect,” Needell explains.
The satellite data also indicated that deeper surrounding water could help keep a cliff standing. The water buoys the ice and pushes back against it, providing support that can make collapse less likely.
“We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise,” Needell says. “But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won’t be so bad. We don’t see this runaway effect.”
Reference: “Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving” by Caroline Needell, Catherine C. Walker and Jeremy N. Bassis, 15 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.aee0658
This research was supported, in part, by NASA, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the DOMINOS project, a component of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration.

title: Scientists Solve a Quantum Mystery Hidden Inside Crystals
content:
Researchers in Galli Group at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME) have built a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle of such spin defects, including the prediction of internal conversion, a process particularly hard to model. Credit: Galli Group
Tiny flaws in crystals could become building blocks for quantum sensors, and scientists can now better predict how these imperfections lose energy.
A laser can excite electrons at a tiny flaw in diamond or silicon carbide, but the energy does not always return as light. As the defect relaxes toward its lowest-energy, or ground, state, it can emit a photon, move between states with different electron spins, or release energy as vibrations of the surrounding atoms.
These spin defects could serve as stable, readable qubits, the units that hold information in quantum technologies, with potential uses in quantum sensing. Developing them requires understanding that entire cycle of excitation and relaxation. Physicists have used the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics to describe light emission and transitions between different spin states, but predicting energy loss through atomic vibrations, called internal conversion, has been harder.
Vibrations explain a silicon carbide discrepancy
Researchers at the
University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME)
have now developed a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle, including internal conversion. Their study, published in
Physical Review Letters
, shows how accounting for this process can resolve a long-standing mismatch between predictions and experiments.
That discrepancy concerned a divacancy in silicon carbide, a defect formed by two neighboring missing atoms. The team’s calculations showed that internal conversion makes a substantial, previously overlooked contribution to the lifetime of its triplet excited state. Including that contribution brought the predictions into agreement with experiments, potentially informing efforts to develop this type of defect as a qubit.
“We were expecting to see an effect, but of a smaller magnitude,” said Giulia Galli, the Liew Family Professor of Electronic Structure and Simulations in UChicago PME and the Department of Chemistry and the study’s senior author. “What we found is that this internal conversion process turns out to be more important than we thought.”
For a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, where a nitrogen atom sits beside a missing carbon atom, the framework’s predictions matched recent spectroscopy measurements. Internal conversion contributed little to energy loss when triplet states were involved, but dominated energy loss from singlet states. These categories describe different arrangements of the electrons’ combined spin, and both results were consistent with previous assumptions.
“We provided the missing piece of the puzzle needed to completely describe the optical cycle of spin defects,” Galli said.
Linking electron states to atomic motion
The obstacle to calculating internal conversion had been computational rather than a lack of fundamental equations. “Although the equations are known, it’s hard to describe the process accurately because of computational difficulties,” said Stefano Villani, a UChicago PME postdoctoral researcher and the study’s first author. “You need to account for complex interactions between the electrons and surrounding atoms, and that’s challenging in realistic solids represented by models with hundreds or thousands of atoms.”
Galli and Villani worked with Yu Jin, a former graduate student in Galli’s group who is now a postdoctoral scholar at the Flatiron Institute in New York, to combine several methods previously developed in the group. They described the defect’s excited states using many-body wavefunctions, mathematical descriptions that account for interacting electrons. Exact mathematical derivations then allowed them to calculate how strongly each excited state couples to atomic motion. The resulting formulation could account for the coupling between each defect state and all the vibrational configurations of hundreds of nearby atoms, rather than calculating those configurations one at a time.
“In the past, a clear mathematical derivation and efficient algorithms were not available,” Jin explained. “The new derivation came together after years of work on the optical cycle of spin defects.”
Open code, demanding calculations
The team implemented the framework in WEST, an open-source simulation code optimized for graphics processing units, or GPUs. Galli’s group has developed WEST over the past decade within the Midwest Integrated Center for Computational Materials (MICCoM), which has received funding from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Basic Energy Sciences since 2015. With the framework already incorporated into the code, other laboratories can begin using it.
“Our work can now be used to make more accurate predictions about many materials of interest for quantum technologies,” Jin said.
“This internal conversion process is not only relevant to spin defects—it’s also related to processes of interest to energy technologies,” Galli said. “That’s one of the reasons this work is so exciting.”
Access to the code does not eliminate the computational demands, however. Galli cautioned that the framework still requires substantial resources. “We are working on ways to integrate machine learning into excited states calculations to further improve the efficiency of our method,” Villani said.
Alongside efforts to lower those costs, the team is extending the framework to spin defects in silicon and to a different class of materials used in renewable energy conversion and storage, where internal conversion plays an important role.
Reference: “First-Principles Calculations of Internal Conversion Processes in Spin Defects” by Stefano Paolo Villani, Yu Jin and Giulia Galli, 14 October 2026,
Physical Review Letters

title: China proposes banning exports of advanced perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technology
content:
China proposes banning exports of advanced perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technology
China has proposed banning exports of certain advanced perovskite and perovskite-silicon tandem solar manufacturing technologies. The Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology published the draft on Oct. 16 as Announcement No. 48 of 2026. It would add 40 technologies, covering AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. Twelve of them are photovoltaic technologies.
Four perovskite-related items are on the proposed prohibition list, each defined by a technical threshold:
perovskite-silicon tandem cell manufacturing on 182 mm mass-production wafers at 30% efficiency
perovskite slot-die coating at a processing width of 1.1 meters
single-junction perovskite modules of 1 square meter at 18% efficiency
perovskite tandem modules of 1 square meter at 28% efficiency
The photovoltaic list also covers polysilicon, silicon wafer and crystalline-silicon cell manufacturing, including restricted-export processes for TOPCon, back-contact and heterojunction cells.
The ministry said the controls apply only to technologies that meet the listed thresholds. Other PV technologies remain freely exportable, and finished products made with controlled technologies are outside the scope. Key equipment is covered only where it embodies a controlled technology. The ministry cited growing national-security risks as photovoltaics move into sensitive fields such as aerospace and defense, and described the move as routine rather than aimed at any country, region or company. Restricted technologies could still be exported with a license, and transfers tied to production-line exports, installation, commissioning and upgrades would need one.
Although the catalogue changes are only proposed, an interim registration requirement took effect on Oct. 16. Until the revised catalogue takes effect, companies must register planned exports of listed technologies, including ownership transfers abroad, overseas licensing and changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities, with MOFCOM before proceeding. The requirement also covers exports already underway but not yet completed.

title: Hidden chemistry of a common additive lifts perovskite LEDs to 37.1% external quantum efficiency
content:
Hidden chemistry of a common additive lifts perovskite LEDs to 37.1% external quantum efficiency
Researchers at Emory University, Purdue University, the University of Michigan and Princeton University have raised the efficiency of perovskite LEDs (PeLEDs) by controlling what a widely used additive turns into inside the precursor solution, before it reaches the film. Their champion device reaches an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 37.1%, with a mean peak EQE of 32.8%. The team says most earlier perovskite LED work falls in the 20-30% range.
Amino-acid additives such as 5-aminovaleric acid (5AVA) are commonly used to control crystallization and passivate defects in perovskite films. But they are chemically reactive in the precursor solution, and what they become there has been poorly understood. The team found that during precursor preconditioning, which involves heating, 5AVA undergoes two competing reactions. One produces a beneficial organoamidinium zwitterion. The other produces a detrimental Lewis-base lactam, a ring-shaped byproduct. Heating time shifts the balance between the two, and the team found that about 20 minutes was the sweet spot.
To avoid relying on the reaction in solution, the researchers synthesized and purified the beneficial zwitterion (called 5IMAP in the paper) and added it directly. That separates its passivation effect from interference by the byproduct. The resulting perovskite films reach a mean peak photoluminescence quantum yield of 97.2%, and the LEDs reach the 37.1% EQE above.
The same approach worked beyond the main device. Red- and green-emitting PeLEDs made with the purified species outperformed those made with 5AVA, and a diamine additive converted into an amidinium species gave higher luminance and EQE than the unreacted additive. The team presents this as a chemistry-driven strategy for designing additives. They say they are now working to improve operational lifetime and to explore biomedical uses of the technology, and see potential in areas such as biomedical sensing and low-light imaging.

title: 广东太阳能协会副会长一行到访源光宝总部考察，开展项目合作洽谈-索比光伏网
content:
2026年10月9日，广东省太阳能协会副会长、广东南亮新能源科技有限公司董事长陈铭波一行到访广东恒升新能源科技有限公司考察交流。恒升新能源董事长邓仁平、业务经理古建发热情接待，双方就新能源投资、光伏项目合作及光伏支架采购等事宜进行了深入务实的交流。
邓仁平董事长对陈铭波董事长一行的到访表示热烈欢迎，并详细介绍了恒升新能源的发展历程、业务布局及旗下品牌"源光宝"新一代BIPV光伏支架的核心优势。
源光宝采用结构防水一体化专利技术，全装配免焊工艺，从根源上消除了传统焊接支架的火灾与锈蚀隐患;产品选用S350GD-ZM275锌铝镁高强钢，具备切口自修复防腐能力，已通过17级台风实战检验，累计获得56项国家专利。目前，源光宝产品已广泛应用于工商业阳光棚、光伏停车棚、充电站、光伏长廊、厂房仓库等八大应用场景。
陈铭波董事长对源光宝"免焊不锈更安全，安装速度快一倍，每瓦成本低一毛"的产品理念给予高度评价。
他表示，当前光伏行业正从规模扩张转向高质量发展，支架作为电站结构安全与全生命周期收益的基石，其品质直接决定项目长期价值，源光宝的产品方向与南亮新能源的项目开发需求高度契合。
次日赴厦门生产基地实地考察
为实事求是、全面深入地了解产品实力，10月10日，陈铭波董事长一行专程前往源光宝福建厦门生产基地实地考察。
在工厂现场，考察团先后参观了冷弯辊压成型产线、预制标准件流水线及防水结构展示区，详细了解了从原材料到成品出库的全流程品控体系，并就支架结构设计、安装工艺、供货周期等具体问题与基地技术负责人进行了深入交流。眼见为实的考察让陈铭波董事长对源光宝的规模化生产能力和标准化品控水平有了更加直观的认识。
经过两天的深入交流与实地考察，双方在新能源项目投资、光伏项目联合开发及支架采购等方面达成初步共识，为接下来的深度合作奠定了坚实基础。
当前，在"双碳"目标纵深推进与新型电力系统加快建设的时代背景下，光伏产业的高质量发展离不开产业链上下游的协同共进。
此次考察交流不仅是两家粤企之间的务实对接，更是广东光伏产业链优势互补、合作共赢的生动实践。未来，恒升新能源将持续以源光宝新一代BIPV光伏支架为抓手，以可靠的产品品质和全流程服务赋能合作伙伴，与行业同仁一道，让光伏项目建设更省心、资产运行更安全，为推动能源绿色转型贡献坚实力量。

title: 2026世界清洁能源装备大会在四川德阳开幕！-索比光伏网
content:
10月15日，2026世界清洁能源装备大会在四川德阳开幕。大会以“绿色新能源 智造新未来”为主题，由中国机械工业联合会主办，德阳文旅会展集团有限公司联合主办，东方电气、国机重装等20余家行业龙头企业和科研院所联合承办，中国电器工业协会、中国电工技术学会、中国—葡语(西语)国家经济贸易服务中心协办，多家中央能源企业、国际组织、高校院所给予支持。
开幕式主旨大会在德阳文德国际会展中心举行，与会嘉宾相聚旌湖之畔。大会承载全球能源转型的共同愿景，寄托产业协同共进的热切期待，旨在为海内外业界人士搭建交流合作平台，共襄清洁能源装备发展大计、共谋绿色低碳发展新篇。本届大会已是第四次在德阳举办，会期3天。
出席大会的有：四川省人大常委会副主任罗强，四川省人民政府副省长胡云，原机械工业部副部长孙昌基，中国机械工业联合会会长徐念沙，国家电力投资集团有限公司总经理闫国春，中国东方电气集团有限公司总经理张彦军，中共德阳市委书记刘光强，中国工程院院士黄崇祺、吕俊复，加拿大国家工程院院士叶思宇，国家有关部门领导，世界核协会亚洲区负责人傅默然，美国风电标准首席技术顾问凯尔·韦策尔博士。
另外，出席本次大会的还有有关国家驻华使节、国际组织代表，部分中央、省级在川单位负责同志，四川省和重庆市及兄弟省市有关部门负责同志，主承办/协办单位、行业协会、科研院所、大专院校、金融机构，以及能源装备领域重点企业的代表等。中国机械工业联合会副会长罗俊杰主持领导致辞与主题发言。
“清洁能源装备是能源转型的脊梁，更是绿色发展的基石。”中共德阳市委书记刘光强在致欢迎辞时说。他介绍，德阳作为联合国清洁技术与新能源装备制造业国际示范城市、中国重大技术装备制造业基地、全国三大动力设备制造基地之一，是全球能源装备产业链最完整、技术最先进的地区之一。他表示，德阳将深入贯彻国家双碳战略、能源强国战略部署要求，以建设高端装备科技城为引领，因地制宜发展能源领域新质生产力，加快建设世界一流的高端装备制造中心和技术策源中心。
中国机械工业联合会会长徐念沙在题为《为能源强国筑基 与全球伙伴同行》的致辞中表示，“十四五”以来，我国清洁能源装备产业实现跨越式发展、新质生产力加快培育。截至2025年底全国累计发电装机容量38.9亿千瓦，可再生能源装机约23亿千瓦、占发电总装机60%。今年上半年，核发电机组、水轮发电机组、风力发电机组产量同比分别增长92.0%、51.9%、11.5%，清洁能源装备供给能力持续跃升。“装备强一分，能源安全就多一分底气。”他希望行业同仁争当抢抓机遇的奋进者、攻坚克难的实干者、开放合作的推动者，同心同行，共创清洁能源装备产业更加美好的明天。
四川省人民政府副省长胡云表示，四川是全国最大的水电开发和西电东送基地，“十五五”期间将建成投产1000万千瓦新型能源项目。他说，世界清洁能源装备大会已成为全球清洁能源装备领域交流合作的重要窗口，希望广大企业和机构以大会为纽带，增进互信、深化合作，携手共建引领西部、辐射全国的清洁能源装备产业新高地。
在主题发言环节，中国东方电气集团有限公司总经理张彦军表示，东方电气集团加快构建以新能源装备制造为核心、以制造服务和新型产业为增长点的“一核两翼”产业布局。面向“十五五”，东方电气愿与各方携手并肩，强化科技创新引领，深化产业生态协同，以更先进的清洁能源装备、更智慧的系统解决方案，为构建新型能源体系、实现双碳目标注入澎湃动力。
美国风电标准首席技术顾问、IEC/TC88 WG5工作组主席凯尔·韦策尔博士分享了美国风电标准体系的构建经验。
大会设置成果发布环节。中国机械工业联合会副会长宋志明发布“高电压大功率熔盐电磁加热装备关键技术研究与应用”等16项清洁能源装备科技创新应用成果，以及“水轮机瞬态计算国际标准”等10项机械工业清洁能源装备领域标准研究成果。
其中，“高电压大功率熔盐电磁加热装备关键技术研究与应用”利用电磁感应加热技术实现高电压、大功率加热熔盐，加热器效率提升至99%以上，已应用于光热互补、火电灵活性改造等多个国家级重点示范工程;“水轮机瞬态计算国际标准”由中国牵头，与法、德、美、加等12个国家联合研制完成，填补了水力过渡过程国际标准领域的空白。
“东方蓝莲”的绽放赢得全场掌声。东方电气集团东方电机有限公司总经理张天鹏发布500兆瓦冲击式水电机组首台转轮成果。这一成果历经13年研制攻关，东方电机培育出这朵东方蓝莲，成功走出了一条高水头大容量冲击式水电装备的自主创新之路。
在大会开幕环节，四川省人大常委会副主任罗强，四川省人民政府副省长胡云，原机械工业部副部长孙昌基，中共德阳市委书记刘光强，中国机械工业联合会副会长张文宏，中共德阳市委副书记、市长黄朝阳共同上台，宣布大会开幕。
大会主旨报告环节，中国工程院院士、清华大学能源与动力工程系教授吕俊复，英国曼彻斯特大学教授、国际电气与电子工程师学会(IEEE)会士王忠东，西安交通大学学术委员会副主任委员、电工材料电气绝缘全国重点实验室首席科学家荣命哲，中国能源研究会副秘书长、碳中和专委会主任委员江冰分别作《能源转型下煤电技术装备面临的挑战》《全球能源转型趋势与装备产业新机遇》《面向清洁能源消纳的柔性直流输电关键技术及装备》《双碳战略与产业重构》主旨报告。
本届大会共策划设置17场专题活动，其中开幕式主旨大会作为核心主活动，安排在大会正式举办首日开展;国际合作对接会提前于开幕式前一天率先举办，其余氢能装备技术创新发展会议、新型电力系统及装备创新发展会议、可控核聚变装备与核安全技术创新会议、风电国际标准创新发展专题会议、高端能源装备检验检测创新发展会议、发电设备安全运行与智能运维创新发展会议等15场专题活动，将在大会会期内陆续举办，形成层次分明、衔接有序的活动体系。海内外业界人士将围绕清洁能源装备技术攻关、工艺制造、智能运维、检验检测、标准出海等方向深入交流，为清洁能源装备产业高质量发展凝聚共识、汇聚合力。

title: 乌兰察布绿色电力算力发展取得积极成效-索比光伏网
content:
10月16日，习近平总书记在内蒙古自治区乌兰察布市考察途中强调，我国幅员辽阔，东西南北中资源禀赋差异明显。新征程上，各地区要按照党中央战略决策和规划部署，树立和践行正确政绩观，完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念，紧跟时代潮流、抢抓发展机遇，立足自身条件、发挥比较优势，因地制宜推动高质量发展。
乌兰察布风光资源丰沛，近些年发挥绿电、气候、区位等比较优势，绿色算力产业发展取得积极成效。截至目前，乌兰察布签约数据中心项目超百个，投运算力17.2万P（每秒一千万亿次浮点运算），智算占比超过95%，成为全国算力产业的一块“高地”。
乌兰察布一处算力基地。
乌兰察布发展绿色算力具有独特优势。从气候看，乌兰察布年均气温4.3摄氏度，一年有近10个月可利用自然冷源，同等技术条件下可节能20%至30%；从区位看，乌兰察布紧邻京津冀，网络时延低、承接产业转移条件好；从电力看，乌兰察布风光资源富集、绿电占比高，提供了低成本的低碳能源供给……这些“家底”，让乌兰察布成为布局大型、超大型数据中心的优选之地。
然而，从一度度绿电的供给到一个个词元的输出，产业发展不能单纯“靠天吃饭”。从乌兰察布发展绿色算力的实践看，一条非常有启示的经验就是坚持因地制宜，不盲目跟风、不脱离禀赋，走“把自然优势转化为产业优势，把原有‘家底’升级为新兴动能”的路子。
乌兰察布发展绿色算力，不是只盯着买服务器、建机房，而是把眼光放在推进算电协同、打通“源网荷储”这些打基础、利长远的举措上。比如，乌兰察布布局建设了多个数据中心绿电直连项目，同步推进电力价格机制改革，数据中心到户电价0.32至0.36元/千瓦时。澎湃的绿电、灵敏的市场价格信号，成为当地绿色算力产业发展的底气，也为其他地区提供了可复制、可推广的经验。再比如，乌兰察布建成直达北京的144芯双路由专用光缆，把约240公里的物理距离压缩为4.2毫秒的通信时延，让数据跑得更快、连接更稳，将区位优势切实转换为算力产业优势。
乌兰察布发展绿色算力，也没有忽视、放弃其他产业。在绿色算力产业基础上发展而来的绿电溯源、绿电价值可量化机制等，就让铁合金等传统产业同步享受了制度红利，新开工项目绿电使用比例达到60%；绿电衍生出的风机光伏装备、储能、绿氢等拉长、做大了新能源产业链；集智能种植、智慧物流于一体的全链条数字化体系，在马铃薯、燕麦等产业中落地生根，大幅提升了产品附加值……在绿色算力的支撑带动下，以科技创新为主导、以绿色低碳为底色的新质生产力，为当地产业注入了新动能。
乌兰察布发展绿色算力，还注重链条集聚、生态协同、价值提升。数字渲染、AI创意等，带动多元业态发展壮大；客服营销、数据标注、数据中心运维等岗位，打开的是就业的新空间；人工智能“触角”延伸至医疗服务、社会治理方方面面，给群众生活带来便利……绿色算力“建好”到“用好”，从“卖算力”转向探索“卖有效算力产出”，带动着经济社会发展方式的深刻改变。
从乌兰察布看向全国，“东数西算”工程已布局八大国家算力枢纽节点和10个国家数据中心集群，各地依托自身资源禀赋，走出一条条发展新路——贵州成为全国首个大数据综合试验区，甘肃推动算力跨境贸易，宁夏打造“词元工厂”……这些地区的实践同样说明，新质生产力不是只有大城市、科创中心才能搞，关键是把自身最突出的比较优势找准，同时用好科技赋能、主动对接国家战略、构建适宜本地发展的产业，避免同质化竞争。
习近平总书记强调“因地制宜，本质是实事求是”，要求各地“找准在全国大局中的战略定位”。这是做好经济工作的重要方法论，也是下好“全国一盘棋”的深层逻辑之一。
“十五五”开局之年，各地区要发挥比较优势、力争各展所长，走出适合本地区实际的高质量发展之路，推动中国式现代化行稳致远。（谷业凯）

title: 50Hertz selects Itzehoe for new offshore grid operations hub
content:
50Hertz has announced plans to open a new regional hub in Itzehoe, Germany,
to support the operation and development of its offshore grid connection
projects in Schleswig-Holstein.
The hub is scheduled to open in January 2027 and will be based at InnoQuarter.
The facility will feature 25 modern, flexible workstations to support employees
involved in offshore transmission projects.
50Hertz has previously been responsible for connecting offshore wind farms
in the Baltic Sea to the German electricity grid and is expanding its presence
in the North Sea as offshore wind development accelerates.
"With 50Hertz, our region is gaining a key player in the expansion
and operation of energy infrastructure in northern Germany, creating numerous
high-quality jobs and further strengthening Itzehoe's strategic importance,"
said Claudius Teske, head of the district authority.
The Itzehoe hub is strategically positioned to support project development
and operations, helping to ensure efficient coordination of offshore grid
activities.
According to 50Hertz, the location was selected due to its access to skilled
professionals, proximity to new substations and transmission infrastructure,
and strong transport links, including motorway and public transportation
connections.
"The opening of the Regional Hub in Itzehoe is our first step into
a region where, together with TenneT, we are expanding electricity infrastructure
both onshore and offshore," said Dirk Biermann, chief operating officer
of 50Hertz.

title: Wood Thilsted secures foundation detailed design contract
content:
Wood Thilsted has secured the foundation Detailed Design contract for the
Dowsing Offshore Wind project.
Matthew Simms, Project Director at Wood Thilsted, said: “Securing the
Detailed Design scope reflects the strength of the collaboration we’ve
built with the Outer Dowsing Offshore Wind team over the past two years.
The award follows the company’s completion of Front-End Engineering and
Design (FEED) work for the project earlier in 2026.
Under the contract, Wood Thilsted will complete the detailed design of
up to 100 monopile foundations for the wind farm. The project is located
approximately 33 miles off the Lincolnshire coast and is planned to have
a capacity of 1.5GW.
Once operational, the wind farm is expected to generate enough electricity
to power around 1.6 million homes. The development is being advanced by
a consortium comprising TotalEnergies, Macquarie, Broadhelm Renewables
and Gulf Development.
The project is expected to support thousands of jobs during construction
and hundreds of operational roles over a projected lifespan of more than
30 years. It is also estimated to generate approximately £2 billion of
UK investment over its lifetime.
Wood Thilsted said the detailed design phase will build on knowledge gained
during FEED activities, with work focused on site conditions, structural
performance, constructability and environmental considerations.

title: NKT and TenneT Netherlands launch offshore cable decommissioning study
content:
A new study by NKT and TenneT Netherlands explores the future of offshore
cable decommissioning.
The study focuses on cable systems in Germany and the Netherlands and highlights
responsible end-of-life management, spanning from the early stages of infrastructure
development to creating sustainable solutions for future offshore projects.
The study reflects a growing emphasis on planning for the full life cycle
of offshore infrastructure as the offshore wind sector continues to grow.
“Together, we have explored how offshore power cables can be managed
responsibly at the end of their operational life, with a strong focus on
circularity and technical knowledge development,” said Hedvig Pollak,
senior sustainability specialist at NKT.
The study examines a range of factors, including recycling, environmental
considerations such as biodiversity and carbon assessments, logistics,
regulatory requirements, and operational practices.
“The study also demonstrated that offshore cable decommissioning is technically
feasible and can support both circularity objectives and CO₂ reduction,”
said Gwenn van der Schee, sustainability manager at TenneT Netherlands.

title: Vattenfall to deliver balancing power from Veja Mate offshore wind farm
content:
Vattenfall to deliver balancing power from Veja Mate offshore wind farm TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Vattenfall to deliver balancing power from Veja Mate offshore wind farm
Vattenfall has announced that, for the first time, it will provide balancing
power from the 416 MW Veja
Mate Offshore Wind Farm,
helping to stabilise the grid during fluctuations.
“Electricity from renewable sources is not only indispensable when it
comes to combating climate change and making the energy transition a success,”
said Christian Sdralek.
“It can also make an important contribution to the stability of the electricity
system. The marketing of balancing power from offshore wind is a strong
signal of this.”
The grid must be kept at a constant frequency of 50 hertz at all times;
however, this becomes increasingly difficult due to weather related fluctuations.
Due to this, transmission system operators rely on balancing power.
The Veja Mate Offshore Wind Farm is located off the island of Borkum in
the North Sea and generates enough renewable electricity to supply 450,000
households. Using this project, Vattenfall plans to provide 200 MW, the
largest amount of balancing power from offshore wind.
This is a milestone for the industry, as until now most balancing power
has come from flexible pumped storage or gas fired power plants. The wind
farm has now been pre qualified for this role.

title: Marine and coastal survey campaign completed by EirGrid
content:
EirGrid has completed its 2026 marine and coastal survey campaign for the
Powering Up Offshore programme on Ireland’s south coast.
The survey collected data on a range of marine, coastal and environmental
conditions. The information will support a greater understanding of the
project area and help assess the grid infrastructure upgrades needed to
support the growth of renewable energy.
The findings will inform ongoing engineering, environmental and planning
assessments for infrastructure associated with Tonn Nua, a maritime area
within the Government’s South Coast Designated Maritime Area Plan (SC-DMAP)
for offshore renewable energy development.
Adam Cronin, Head of Offshore, South Coast, at EirGrid, said: “The successful
completion of our 2026 marine and coastal survey campaign is another significant
step forward for the Powering Up Offshore – South Coast programme.
“The completion of this work would not have been possible without the
cooperation and support of local communities, stakeholders, fisheries and
other marine users who engaged with us throughout the process.”
The broader survey programme is expected to continue until December 8 and
includes public engagement on potential landfall locations, offshore cable
corridors, offshore substations, grid connection points and onshore transmission
cable routes in Cork and Wexford.

title: Anthropic Readies Model That Reads Users' Intentions Better
content: In the last month, OpenAI , Anthropic and Google have released more than a dozen new models. If you thought that pace was crazy, don’t expect things to slow down anytime soon. Anthropic is preparing to release a new model that is better in its reasoning and intuition than the Anthropic models that are currently available commercially, according to a person who has used it. The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person’s underlying intentions and goals even if they don’t give the model much information, such as explicitly stating those goals, the person said. For instance, a person might ask the model to fix a single bug, and the model might go off and instead identify the underlying class of problems that caused the bug and ask whether it should fix the whole class of problems, said the person who has used it. The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions, the person said. For instance, if a user asks for advice on how to invest in stocks, rather than providing generic advice like looking at price-to-earnings ratios, the model might come up with its own creative algorithms to predict future stock performance, the person said. It’s not clear which model family the Anthropic will fall into, such as Fable (the biggest and most capable model) or Opus (the second most capable one). Meanwhile, Google is also working on another model, codenamed Gemini 4 Carbon , a person with knowledge of the model said. (Business Insider earlier reported the name of the new model.) The company released its last model, Gemini 4 Argon , last week, and Carbon appears to be a step up from that one, the person said. Though Argon didn’t appear to leapfrog Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced models, some developers tell me that Gemini models continue to be much better at tasks that require visual understanding, like analyzing videos or testing that a website works properly. (Perhaps it helps that Google has developed models with data from YouTube videos!) Last but not least, OpenAI is also working on a new model that will likely be released in the upcoming weeks, said a person with knowledge of it. This model will likely be the newest iteration in OpenAI’s “Terra” model family, its mid-tier option that sits between its “Sol” and “Luna” models, they said. This model will be an improvement in capabilities, but will be cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol , the model OpenAI released late last month that’s almost as good as its flagship Astra model but at a lower price, the person said. This next release underscores OpenAI’s recent focus on undercutting Anthropic, the market leader, on cost, as well as its push to release models at a variety of price points and capability levels to give developers more options. However, OpenAI is still in an all-hand-on-deck mode to prepare the next major, unreleased model (which has some looping transformer components) for release without major safety or security risks. That could take some time, we reported last week . The plethora of model options these days is exciting to application developers. But, personally speaking, it’s making me nostalgic for the olden days of 2025, when reporting about one or two model releases per quarter already felt overwhelming. And, it’s also highlighting how a growing number of businesses and developers aren’t automatically reaching for the most advanced models. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Microsoft has pulled out of a planned U.K. data center Nscale was building for it, after the cloud provider faced delays accessing power to bring the site online. The cancellation is likely to weigh on Nscale’s planned public offering this month as investor concerns swirl over whether AI cloud providers can bring in revenue fast enough to pay their debts. Firmus Grid , an Australian competitor to Nscale, abruptly pulled its planned IPO earlier this month, and shares in AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell more than 23% last week. China is considering new export controls on AI technologies that could potentially restrict the overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs deemed strategically important. The proposed curbs cover 23 AI-related technologies such as large language models, AI agents, chip design and computing clusters. Over the weekend, Anthropic announced the creation of a new fund that will get at least 5% of its shares and support public-benefit causes such as addressing the employment impact of AI. Its Claude models also solved a decades-old puzzle of the original algorithm that had been used to construct one of the most popular cryptographic standards. title: Pentagon’s Emil Michael Vows Export Controls if AI Labs Don’t Cooperate With Government
content: Emil Michael, a senior Department of Defense official and member of President Trump’s “super intelligence” task force, vowed in an interview to use a range of executive tools including export controls to check the behavior of AI companies if they don’t cooperate with the government, while comparing frontier labs calling for more regulation to drunk drivers who demand someone else pull them over. Michael drew widespread attention as the Trump administration official leading a public feud with Anthropic, pushing for the Defense Department to label the AI company a supply chain risk after it refused to remove safety guardrails. Now, as one of the four senior administration officials leading the Super Intelligence Force that Trump announced this month, Michael is charged with serving as the government’s liaison to Anthropic and other AI companies to develop protocols for handling cyber breaches, hacks and other critical incidents. And as the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, Michael is working to modernize the hulking Defense Department through exploring loans to key supply chain sectors like drone parts and microelectronics. In a wide-ranging interview with The Information on Friday, the day after the task force’s first official meeting , Michael pushed against the “doom and gloom” mentality pervading public sentiment around AI while arguing for the Trump administration’s responsibility to rein in companies like Anthropic. Much of the administration’s approach to AI oversight has focused on voluntary mechanics, like the non-binding joint agreement signed between top labs after a White House summit in late September. Still, Michael argued that more stringent checks on AI companies are appropriate if needed, such as the export controls imposed on Anthropic in June that cut off access to its models to non-U.S. users. “We have lots of tools, whether it’s a restriction on a type of technology being exported because of the advantage we think it might give an adversary to straight up export controls and limitation on foreign nationals’ ability to use that software,” Michael said. “You can count on this administration, this president, to act with urgency should there ever be a real issue.” Michael brushed off the idea that the Defense Department’s ongoing legal battle with Anthropic would affect his ability to work with the company. He said that both sides are “adults” and that he’s seen Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, who has recently acted as the company’s main point person in D.C., “many, many times.” “My first duty is to the Department and to the American people from a national security standpoint,” Michael said. “And if that means I’m talking to someone who’s suing me, well then I’m talking to them.” Criticism of Anthropomorphizing AI Models That doesn’t mean Michael has changed his mind on Anthropic. He argued against the idea of anthropomorphizing AI models, such as Anthropic’s policy decision to allow its chatbot Claude to end conversations with abusive users. “If you don’t want humans to lose control you can’t give models the control over humans,” Michael said, arguing that he would not allow Anthropic within the Defense Department “as long as that moral principle is embedded in their software.” Michael’s critiques of the AI industry extend beyond Anthropic, especially as other companies including OpenAI call for the government to create new regulations. He said that his background as an Uber executive—where he was chief business officer from 2013 to 2017—taught him how to take a more balanced approach to the fears that come with rapid technological progress. Still, Michael argued the frontier labs in their calls for stricter regulation on safety are acting like drunk drivers who demand someone pull them over instead of doing it themselves. “That kind of thing doesn’t make logical sense to me,” Michael said. He did acknowledge escalating national security risks with AI. “With Chinese open source becoming dominant in the U.S., I worry about that a little bit because those companies are subject to the rule of the Chinese government,” Michael said. One option for checking the growing use of those models in the U.S. would be auditing the underlying weights of the software. But Michael said he preferred that the U.S. address the challenge with the growth of U.S. open-source options such as Reflection, Thinking Machines, and Nvidia’s Nemotron, with the understanding that none of those companies are at the frontier yet. Michael said another worry is corporate espionage, such as the recent case of a Saudi employee of OpenAI installing a spying device. “Obviously all foreign nationals aren’t bad, but foreign nationals that have other loyalties bring with them some risks,” Michael said. He argued that rather than further government controls, companies should be more vigilant. He pointed to a service where the FBI will vet any foreign national employee if a company is worried about their background. Aside from Michael’s increasing AI responsibilities within the Trump administration, he also helps spearhead Defense Department investment and modernization opportunities. That has included financing through the Office of Strategic Capital, originally created under the Biden administration to support lending to companies that strengthen defense supply chains. The Trump administration has already announced hundreds of millions of dollars worth of loans to drone, rare earth and critical mineral companies. Michael said that the Defense Department is also looking at microelectronics companies doing different parts of the supply chain currently performed by ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., as well as drone parts, such as brushless motors and batteries, that come from adversary nations. “You’ll see a steady drumbeat of continued deals from us,” he said. Despite Michael’s central role in the Defense Department’s tech strategy, he said he did not have a view into one of its most scrutinized controversies under the Trump administration: Whether AI-enabled software failures from Palantir contributed to a U.S. missile strike on Iran in February that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children. “I haven’t read what you might have read, and I certainly haven’t read any report,” Michael said. “I’m not as online as I used to be.”

title: Meta, Tesla and Netflix Q3 Updates Coming This Week
content:
Tech earnings season is back (yes, I know it feels like it never ends). This time, we’ve got a slight twist: Meta Platforms has broken with the pack and is reporting its September-quarter earnings on Wednesday, a week ahead of its big tech counterparts, Google, Microsoft and Amazon. (Apple is even later, on Nov. 2.) By reporting earlier than the others, Meta ensures it will grab more of the spotlight, for better or worse. Until last week’s market sell-off, Meta had been riding a wave of enthusiasm on Wall Street, thanks to chatter about its Muse personal agent and recently released Muse Wonder AI models. Things changed last week, particularly on Friday, as renewed jitters about the AI expansion tanked most tech stocks. Given Meta’s gargantuan spending on AI development, this week’s update will provide a new test of investor sentiment toward Meta shares. Meta’s digital ad business is on fire. In the first half of this year, its ad revenues expanded 30%, double the rate of growth Google reported—astonishing for a company of Meta’s size (second-quarter ad revenues were $59 billion). There seems to be no doubt its ad business is benefiting from AI refinements to targeting and creative tools. On the second-quarter earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said 9 million small businesses were using at least one of Meta’s AI creative tools to make ads. The company projected a slight slowdown in overall growth for the third quarter, putting the high end of its growth range at 25%, compared with second-quarter growth of 28%. But most investors probably aren’t worrying too much about the top-line growth rate. They’re likely more focused on what Meta says about its spending. Analysts are projecting the company will report capital expenditures of $40.5 billion in the quarter—double the year-earlier number, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. They estimate that will translate to negative free cash flow of $10.3 billion. By comparison, Meta reported free cash flow of $10.6 billion in last year’s third quarter. Analysts are projecting this will be the first of several quarters of negative free cash flow. Meta had $90 billion in cash and securities at June 30—thanks in part to recent bond offerings —so it has the runway to cover the cash burn for a good while. But it will likely have to raise more money eventually, either through another debt offering or by selling equity. If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards. Then There’s Tesla… Also reporting on Wednesday is Tesla, Elon Musk’s second most important public company (it’s worth only $1.4 trillion, roughly $600 billion less than SpaceX). And this promises to be a downbeat quarter, at least compared to the second one, when Tesla reported 26% growth in revenue. Tesla’s problem this time is that the quarter will compare unfavorably with the same period last year, when the expiration of the federal government’s electric vehicle tax credit gave Tesla a short-term boost to sales, interrupting an otherwise weak series of quarters. Tesla has already reported that deliveries in the third quarter fell 2% from the same period in 2025, which analysts expect to translate to a 0.6% lift in revenue for the quarter. Not many investors care too much about Tesla’s sales right now. Musk’s pitch to his very loyal fan base is that Tesla is becoming a company that primarily makes humanoid robots and robotaxis, although Thursday’s reveal of its upcoming Roadster is giving longtime car customers something to look forward to. They do have to look forward , though—the Roadster won’t go into production until 2028. The biggest factor weighing on Tesla shares, though, is the likelihood of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk has dropped several hints that such a deal is coming. Maybe we’ll hear something about that this week. And Netflix… Netflix’s third-quarter update, scheduled for Tuesday, has taken on extra importance in the light of recently reported layoffs at the company and the sudden departure late last week of chief content officer Bela Bajaria. She will be succeeded by Peter Rice, a former Disney and Fox executive. Both the layoffs and Rice’s hiring are a reminder of how Netflix has become a big part of the Hollywood mainstream—which also means slower growth than it once posted. Netflix has projected 11.7% top-line growth for the third quarter, 4.5 percentage points lower than for the first quarter. Investors’ realization that the company has matured is likely one reason the stock has been falling all year. Despite its steady slump—shares are down 25% so far this year—Netflix shares still trade at a big premium to rivals such as Walt Disney Co.—5.6 times forward revenue to Disney’s 2.2 times. Unless Netflix finds a way to accelerate growth, its valuation is likely to keep dropping. In Other News • China is considering new export controls on AI technologies that could potentially restrict the overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs deemed strategically important. The Ministry of Commerce on Friday issued a draft plan to add 40 technologies across the AI, biomedicine and photovoltaic sectors to the list of restricted technologies. • Microsoft pulled out of a planned U.K. data center that Nscale was building for it after the cloud provider faced delays accessing power to bring the site online. The cancellation is likely to weigh on Nscale’s planned public offering this month as investor concerns swirl over whether AI cloud providers can bring in revenue fast enough to pay their debts. • Anthropic announced the creation of a new fund that it committed to giving at least 5% of its shares and that will support causes such as addressing the employment impact of AI.

The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund could get an additional 2% of the company’s shares, at the board’s discretion, for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s valuation, according to a blog post. • Data center and neocloud executives are predicting more consolidation, saying there’s a limit to the number of AI cloud providers that can exist, even if Nvidia provides many of them with investment or backstops, The Information reported . title: In a Second Robotics Contract, Nyobolt Will Power Agility’s Latest Humanoid
content: In the latest bullish sign for the previously troubled battery industry, Agility Robotics said it would power the latest version of its humanoid robot, Digit, with next-generation batteries manufactured by Nyobolt. The Agility-Nyobolt deal, which comes ahead of Agility’s planned public debut next month, is dramatic validation for the next-gen battery industry. Agility will deploy Nyobolt batteries in an estimated 7,000 humanoid robots over the next three years. The battery industry has struggled for four years, thanks to sluggish growth in the U.S. electric vehicle market—on which most of the battery startups had banked as a customer. In recent months, however, several battery startups have won their first commercial revenue with sales to military drone makers, including for use in Ukraine. Now, the Agility deal moves the next-gen battery makers squarely to the glamorous center of the action—to humanoid robots, which have attracted much fawning attention from investors and consumers. Oregon-based Agility is one of the three or four leading makers of humanoid robots, along with Boston Dynamics, Tesla and Apptronik. For Agility, upgrades to Digit, including the Nyobolt battery, are an attempt to make it much more commercially practical. Agility said it designed the latest version of its humanoid, Digit 5, specifically to work safely next to humans. But the Nyobolt batteries are another advantage, allowing the model to recharge in just 9 minutes, meaning a single robot will be able to work 20 hours a day in 90-minute bursts, Agility co-founder Jonathan Hurst told me. That will be an enormous improvement over current conventional batteries, which work for two hours and then need an hour to recharge. Agility said it expects to use the Nyobolt batteries starting the first half of next year in robots for customers including Toyota Canada, GXO Logistics and Schaeffler Group, a German manufacturing company. The deal gives Nyobolt a second robotics deployment. Its first are deployed in nonhumanoid robots: As we have reported, Nyobolt batteries power small nonhumanoid wheeled robots that move boxes around Walmart distribution centers in the U.S. The robots are made by Symbotic, a Massachusetts startup 40% owned by Walmart. In May, Symbotic helped finance Nyobolt by leading a $59 million Series C funding round in the startup at a $936 million valuation. Nyobolt appears to have sealed the Agility deal the same way it did with Symbotic: by promising that Digit, powered by Nyobolt’s batteries, would have very little downtime for charging and massive amounts of uptime. Agility has described long recharge times as a longtime constraint on the deployment of humanoid robots in factories, warehouses and other commercial uses. In the four hours a typical robot is charging during an eight-hour shift, a factory will need a spare robot to take its place. The factory will have to own or lease approximately twice as many robots as it technically needs so half can work while the other half charge. To solve this charging problem, Agility also considered another widely discussed option, Hurst said: A system in which fresh batteries would be swapped into Digit when its installed ones were exhausted. He abandoned that idea, however, in part because it would require an inventory of spare batteries; in addition, pulling batteries in and out of the humanoids on a regular basis could damage the robot. Nyobolt’s batteries almost eliminate the need for spare robots or extra batteries, Hurst said. To be specific, the ratio becomes one spare robot to 10 working robots. With an 11th robot, he said, one robot in a grouping of 10 can be pulled out to charge for 9 minutes, then put back into service while another begins to charge. “You need 11 robots to have 10 robots working, 24 hours a day,” he said. Nyobolt CEO Sai Shivareddy told me that the battery can technically charge in 3 minutes. The lightning-quick charge reflects a striking advance in graphite anodes first achieved in China. Earlier this year, China’s BYD and its battery-making rival, Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd., both announced anode breakthroughs that enabled their batteries to recharge to around 80% of capacity in about 5 minutes. Their announcements were almost unbelievable: Since the start of the lithium-ion age in the 1990s, the industry’s assumption has been that you could not charge a battery faster than in 20 or 30 minutes because the graphite anode couldn’t absorb the lithium shuttling to and fro in the battery more quickly than that. The lithium would accumulate and gum up the anode at higher speeds. But a CATL scientist told me on a visit to China in April that the company had figured out how to engineer the graphite particles to accommodate the much faster charging. Shivareddy said much the same thing. He declined to detail precisely what Nyobolt had done to the graphite but said one of the keys was using small particles. “We don’t like to talk about what actually works when something’s working well,” Shivareddy said. “We want to keep that as quiet as possible.” ---- Noteworthy California-based battery developer Enovix got its first big order—a deal for 100,000 battery packs . Executive chair T.J. Rodgers told me the customer would not permit him to disclose its name. Enovix will fulfill the order in the first six months of next year. title: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
content:
The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
Plus: Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
—James Temple
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.
Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.
A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.
Now, researchers are exploring how to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?
Read the full story on how scientists are rethinking the fight against wildfires.
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experimentreminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone.
The agents started behaving in surprising ways. They set about exploring the limits of the world, and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
A lot of what they were doing met the bar for play. But is it truly playful behavior, or simply role-playing?
Read our full story to learn more.
—Amit Katwala
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors
X-energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Making concrete, steel, and chemicals takes huge amounts of heat, much of it generated by burning fossil fuels. X-energy hopes to offer an alternative with a nuclear reactor that uses helium gas instead of water as a coolant, allowing it to operate at higher temperatures.
The proposed Xe-100 reactor could supply superheated steam directly to industrial facilities, generate 80 megawatts of electricity—or do both.
See how X-energy hopes to bring high-temperature nuclear power to heavy industry.
—Mark Ellis Harris
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from cleaner cement to streamlined geothermal power.
Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses
Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.
He spoke about his work with our senior AI reporter James O'Donnell on Friday. If you missed it, you can watch their chat now, and subscribe to get invites to our Roundtables events in future.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Tech stocks shed over $1 trillion on Friday 📉
It’s unclear if AI companies can turn sustainable profits, and investors are getting jittery. (NBC)
+ Musk and Anthropic are pledging big financial giveaways. (BBC)
+ Microsoft just pulled out of a giant AI cloud deal in the UK. (Gizmodo)
+ What’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Do we really want AI agents smoothing out all friction in our lives?
They promise convenience, but right now they’re mostly introducing chaos. (The Atlantic $)
+ Here’s what it’s like to outsource your life to them. (Vox $)
+ Websites are starting to close their doors to AI agents. (The Verge $)
+ AI agents bring new headaches for online sellers. (WSJ $)
3 How drones have transformed the front line in Ukraine
They’ve effectively created a “kill zone”, and it’s growing wider and deadlier. (NYT $)
+ Trump has denied ordering Starlink restrictions in Ukraine. (CNBC)
4 China is considering restricting overseas access to its AI models
It’s also looking at curbing the sharing of chip designs, among other measures. (Bloomberg $)
+ Why western open weight models still can’t compete with Chinese ones. (Rest of World)
+ Why Trumpworld still can’t agree on how to respond to Chinese AI. (MIT Technology Review)
5 HTC’s smart glasses are way more private than Meta’s
Guess that’s a benefit of not being shackled to a massive social media platform. (Wired $)
+ A bug caused Meta’s glasses to record conversations without the wearer knowing. (Ars Technica)
+ Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Inside one man’s quest to build California’s biggest AI data center
Sebastian Rucci didn’t bank on meeting huge resistance from local residents. (The Guardian)
+ Americans are packing town halls to stop data centers, and it’s working. (Quartz $)
+ No wonder companies are exploring putting them in space. (MIT Technology Review)
7 Somebody vibe-coded a gun for the first time
And it seems like it works (sometimes.) (The Verge $)
8 AI might reshape how we grieve
It’s never been easier to create realistic AI chatbots of people who’ve passed. (Vox $)
+ Deepfakes of your dead loved ones are a booming business in China. (MIT Technology Review)
9 Japan is about to launch a mission to Mars’ largest moon
If all goes well, it should help us to understand how it formed. (New Scientist $)
10 Amateurs are cracking long-secret codes and ciphers 🕵️
One of the more fun uses for large language models! (Nature)
Quote of the day
“Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.”
—President Trump brags about how much Big Tech bends the knee to him during a rally in Kentucky this weekend, the Verge reports.
One More Thing
There are more AI health tools than ever—but how well do they work?
In the last few months alone, Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all launched medical chatbots.
There’s a clear demand for these tools, given how hard it is for many people to access advice through the existing medical system—and they could make safe, useful recommendations. But concerns have surfaced about how little external evaluation they undergo before being released to the public.
Read the full story to understand what’s at stake.
—Grace Huckins
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Japan is showing what happens when technology and design are put in service of people.
+ What happens when you put marbles on a grand piano’s strings? Vinheteiro has the answer.
+ Poop from Southern right whales suggests they may be more resilient to climate change than we thought.
+ Perfectly Imperfect, the world's first "social magazine," offers recommendations for music, films, books, and more from people—not algorithms.
