title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
content:
In the middle of an
especially warm
July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had
reached 12 feet
in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.
A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.
In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.
Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies
15% of the land
around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.
“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”
Researchers Eric Miller (left) and Alison York (right) record thaw depth at the site of the Yankovich Road Fire.
LEIF VAN CISE
This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.
Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada
released more carbon
than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.
Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.
“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."
Woodwell scientist Brendan Rogers (above) has been studying the impact of Arctic-boreal fires on permafrost, as well as what could be done about it.
PHILIP KEITH (PHOTOS), WOODWELL CLIMATE RESEARCH (MAPS)
Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative
known as North Fire
to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions,
MIT Technology Review
can report.
The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.
Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
‘A massive blind spot’
Emissions from forest fires have risen
60% around the world
since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.
This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.
In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.
“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”
The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores
around 1.5 trillion tons
of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost
since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.
Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and
none incorporate
the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in
earlier this year.
These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.
As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.
2022 paper
Science Advances
, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.
The Yukon Flats pilot
Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.
For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.
It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the
federal and state agencies
responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they
present a direct danger
to communities.
“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented
ideal conditions
for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”
LEIF VAN CISE
LEIF VAN CISE
LEIF VAN CISE
Members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium hike into areas affected by fire to measure the layers of ash left in the soil on the forest floor.
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some
750,000 acres
. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.
But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.
Mapping and modeling
One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. Crucially, excessive efforts to stamp out fires in the past have allowed the buildup of dry plant material that fuels more severe fires later.
“We’re not going after all fires all the time,” says Rogers over lunch in a sunny courtyard on the Stanford University campus, where Woodwell and EDF hosted a workshop on potential fire interventions in January. “We can’t do that. We don’t want to do that. We shouldn’t do that. So how do we prioritize our resources?”
Woodwell and its collaborators are working to answer that question by developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across interior Alaska. The plan is to eventually expand it across much of Canada as well.
These maps will highlight the locations of rich reserves of yedoma and other forms of permafrost, forecast where fires are most likely to break out in the next 10 to 15 years, and predict how they’re likely to behave and spread.
“Our ultimate goal is to get a layer that can tell us, if a fire were to occur, what areas are most vulnerable to high carbon emissions, permafrost thaw, permafrost degradation,” Rogers says.
In response to a question about potentially putting firefighters at risk, Rogers stressed in an email that it’s “a very serious issue that needs careful consideration.”
He added that early fire detection technologies, preventative fire stewardship practices, improved fire suppression planning and other measures can all help to reduce dangers to firefighters as well as communities.
‘Mild fire’
Once areas of particular risk are identified, the first option is to take measures to prevent fires there, or at least to reduce the odds that they’ll become major ones. That generally entails using heavy equipment or intentional, controlled fires to clear away vegetation that could fuel new fires, or to create fire breaks that might check their spread.
A cultural burn earlier this spring in Fort Yukon.
COURTESY OF EDWARD ALEXANDER
Indigenous tribes carried out what’s known as cultural burning
for thousands of years
to reduce fire dangers, clear land for crops, and more. The practice was widely outlawed across North America beginning in the 1800s, though those rules have loosened in recent years.
COURTESY OF EDWARD ALEXANDER
Both cultural and prescribed fires, however, remain controversial because they can
out of control. And even if they remain contained, the fires can still produce smoke that wafts into towns.
But rushing around to put out blazes after they’ve started will never get Alaska ahead of its surging wildfire problem, says Edward Alexander, cochair of the Gwich’in Council International, which represents the Indigenous Gwich’in peoples of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and Alaska.
“There’s not enough money in the world for this to be a chainsaw-and-ax problem,” he says. “This country is too big up here.”
Alexander, who also serves as senior Arctic lead at Woodwell, argues that Alaska should encourage much greater use of cultural burning to reduce the risk of conflagrations and the emissions that come with them.
“We need mild fire, not wildfire,” he says.
New pilot projects
The North Fire initiative will include several additional pilot research projects, including an effort to study the potential for cultural burning to reduce climate and fire dangers near Fort Yukon, Alaska.
The plan is for a wildland firefighting crew operated by the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments, a consortium in the Yukon Flats region, to carry out cultural burns there next spring, Rogers says.
Researchers at Woodwell and the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, will then collect and analyze data flammability, carbon levels, and permafrost over several years, in the hopes of learning more about what such interventions do.
Similarly, the Polis researchers at the University of Victoria plan to study how adding fuel breaks, by logging or switching to less flammable trees, alters fire risks in British Columbia.
The broad aim of the North Fire initiative is to accelerate research and expand community involvement “in a way that helps us scale this as a meaningful global natural climate solution on a rapid timeline,” says Erin Harrington, a partner at the Alaska Venture Fund, a philanthropy focused on environmental, economic development, and Indigenous issues.
Detecting fires from space
Other observers, including Jandt, believe the bigger opportunity to reduce fire emissions and preserve permafrost may lie in the “initial attack.” That means marshalling planes, tankers, and firefighters to stamp fires out at the first sign of them, before they’ve had the chance to turn into conflagrations.
Once fires reach a certain size, it takes much more time to contain them—and the job becomes far more dangerous.
Accelerating response times is one of the chief promises of the
FireSat satellite constellation
, which is expected to begin delivering fire data at least twice daily from around the world to Woodwell, a handful of fire agencies, and other
early adopters
Currently, it can take days to spot fires. But once the full constellation is in place, likely in the early 2030s, FireSat should be capable of detecting and providing updated images of fires anywhere in the world every 20 minutes or less.
The first prototype satellite launched in 2025, and three operational ones went into orbit in July. The Earth Fire Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the constellation, expects to launch four more by the end of next year.
FireSat's prototype satellite captured images from two remote Alaskan wildfires, the Moran and Chicken fires, in the summer of 2025.
A number of similar systems are also coming online. German-based OroraTech
has launched
18 of its fire-detecting satellites in the last year and a half. Similarly, Canadian agencies are planning to launch their own satellite constellation,
dubbed WildFireSat
, beginning in 2029.
But as these systems produce more and more detections across the globe, it’ll become increasingly essential to build tools that can filter through that information.
EDF is supporting and collaborating on several projects that could potentially help with that, and it ultimately intends to develop an AI-powered triage tool that could help fire agencies prioritize responses as FireSat and other fire-spotting tools come online.
"All of this is kind of like building the data ecosystem around FireSat, so that when they start popping out “fire start here, there, fire start here, fire start there,” we won’t be like, ‘Oh shit, there’s fires everywhere,’” Buma says. “We’ll have a framework. It won’t be perfect, obviously. We’ll have to improve it, but we’ll have the machinery to incorporate those data.”
Rapid response
But faster detections and decisions do only so much. Regions would still need to get firefighting personnel and resources to those fires fast enough to prevent them from burning out of control.
“Say we have the full FireSat constellation up and running, and it spots a fire that just broke out in one of these sort of high-priority, highly vulnerable areas,” I said to Rogers and Frumhoff during our conversation in that Stanford courtyard. “How might we deploy firefighting resources to a remote area fast enough for it to matter in that scenario?”
“I think the answer, unfortunately, is that it depends,” Rogers responded.
Ideally, he said, we would have fire management policies in place that allow for putting out fires with a high risk of producing climate-warming emissions. In addition, regions could install more firefighting personnel and resources across more operational centers, strategically placed in locations that allow them to get to those blazes fast.
Frumhoff stresses that Woodwell isn’t promoting any particular companies but says there are additional technologies “in the mix of conversations” that might help to prevent or rapidly put out fires as well.
Those possible approaches include seeding clouds to
suppress lightning strikes
and pre-positioning autonomous firefighting helicopters to respond rapidly to high-emissions-risk fires.
Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is
developing and testing
autonomous versions of the Black Hawk helicopter, equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks. It is collaborating with Rain Industries, a startup based in Alameda, California, that has developed software to track shifting conditions and steer unpiloted aircraft through the process of putting out wildfires.
Last year, Sikorsky and Rain tested their autonomous wildfire suppression technologies during a staged burn in California.
TED CARLSON/RAIN AERO
The company says it has talked to fire agencies and the “broader Alaska fire community” about the potential use of its technology but declined to name any specific entities it has interacted with.
“The twin climate tipping points of the yedoma permafrost and the boreal forest, and the fact that it’s completely underresourced at the moment, from my perspective does make it an ideal use case for autonomous aircraft,” says Max Brodie, chief executive officer of Rain.
Defending carbon
Advancing technologies can only do so much if governments’ fire prevention and suppression policies don’t prioritize preserving carbon.
And that will remain a hard sell given the costs of managing extensive areas of land that nations have historically left largely alone.
The 2022
Science Advances
paper estimated that additional fire suppression efforts would cost about $12.63 per metric ton of prevented carbon dioxide emissions—a number that drops when the carbon in permafrost is taken into account, according to upcoming research.
But that would still add up to about $7 billion in additional spending this decade to keep Alaska’s fire emissions at their historical levels, and another $7 billion to $50 billion over the subsequent 30 years as fire severity continues to rise.
Frumoff stresses that those figures just reflect what the researchers found it would cost to preserve the status quo, which is not necessarily what the policy goal would be.
But widening the scope of where we put out fires will inevitably create a big added cost for fire agencies that are already notoriously underfunded in the US. While Alaska produces about half the nation’s wildfire emissions, it receives
around 4%
of federal firefighting funds.
A wildfire burning about a mile north of Alaska’s Denali National Park on June 30, 2024.
NATIONAL PARK SERVICE VIA AP
The US Wildland Fire Service provided a prepared statement in response to an
MIT Technology Review
inquiry asking whether preserving carbon could or should become a priority in certain fire management decisions. The roundabout reply suggests that this isn’t the agency’s prime concern: “Firefighter and public safety are the top priorities for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.”
Frumhoff says it’s possible that landowners or government agencies could eventually use carbon markets to defray some of the additional costs. Woodwell has also had multiple conversations with Alaska’s federal legislators about the value of preventing catastrophic wildfires and the need to increase the “total pot” of public funding, he says.
Kicking the fire can
A few days after walking through the fire scar in Fairbanks, I drove slowly along a crumpled stretch of Stampede Road, just north of Denali National Park, where the underlying permafrost had melted without the aid of fire.
I arrived at a cramped wooden cabin to meet with Michelle Mack, a regents professor of ecosystem ecology at Northern Arizona University.
Mack studies how fire is altering ecosystems in the high northern latitudes as the region grows warmer and drier, and she sometimes collaborates with Rogers and other scientists working on the push to protect permafrost in other areas of research. But she’s unsure how much these interventions will accomplish as climate change continues.
“I’m an empiricist, and at this point, it’s not clear to me that the empirical evidence suggests that we can actually have any impact on these fires,” she says.
Michelle Mack, a Northern Arizona University professor, studies how fires are affecting permafrost and altering ecosystems across Alaska.
MATT 'MARTIAN' WILLIAMS
She expects there will be clear cases where we could and should act fast to put out fires and “keep carbon in the ground.” She points to the example of the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire, a massive tundra fire on Alaska’s North Slope that might have been extinguished with relative ease in its early days but was instead allowed to burn until the winter snows put it out
nearly three months later
. Over that time, it ripped across 400 square miles and, Mack’s research showed, released
more than 2 million tons
of carbon into the air.
“I feel like that’s the low-hanging fruit, something that doesn’t cost much—and that’s where the technology for detection I think is really important,” she says.
But she adds that fires in boreal forests can rapidly spread in unpredictable ways, frustrating efforts to quickly extinguish them even when they are spotted right away.
In addition, rapidly putting out a fire one season doesn’t necessarily reduce the fire risk for a given forest, so suppression may simply kick the “fire can” down the road—delaying but not preventing an inevitable loss of carbon, Mack says.
Her thinking more recently shifted “a little” after she came across an earlier modeling paper that showed some encouraging findings on the potential of early suppression to reduce the footprint of boreal fires. But she says that prevention through forest thinning, prescribed burns, and the introduction of less flammable deciduous trees to create “living fire breaks” is probably a more promising path than technology-augmented suppression.
“If we could solve this with a techno fix, that’d be great,” she says. “But what if we solved it with nature?”
‘A real difference’
Rogers, in an emailed response to Mack’s concern, said that the interventions they’re exploring, which do include both prevention and suppression, “can make a real difference.”
“I certainly agree that some fires are much easier to suppress via initial attack than others,” he wrote. “That said, until I see data showing me otherwise, I believe there is strong potential to bend the curve with management.”
EDF’s Buma acknowledges there are a number of unknowns, including how quickly agencies could act on faster detections from satellites—and how big the political obstacles will be to making necessary changes to fire management policies.
“We can’t overpromise what’s possible. We don’t know what’s possible,” he says. “It’s all new. But we’re in a new climate and have to consider trying new things.”

title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
content:
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.
Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.
AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.
“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.
The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”
As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)
Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”
Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.
“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”
Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”
“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”
As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.
“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”
“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

title: How far can we push computing?
content:
MIT Technology Review
Explains:
Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next.
You can read more from the series here
On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire
Encyclopædia Britannica
on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.
In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out.
The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.
But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains.
Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.
The descent
During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands.
The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole
Britannica
to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of
A Tale of Two Cities
at the required scale.
The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor.
The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope.
The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law.
Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.
Slowing down
Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling.
SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS
For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed.
Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits.
The ultimate computer
Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate.
These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in
titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.
The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to
, holds about 9 ×10
joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×10
operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today.
The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop.
Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation
waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10
joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch.
Memory density obeys a limit of its own, and this one reaches all the way to gravity. How many bits can a region of space hold? In 1981, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein, while working out the thermodynamics of black holes, determined the amount: The information inside any bounded region is limited by its size and the energy it contains. For a region the size of Lloyd’s ultimate laptop, that comes to about 10
bits, some 10
to a cubic millimeter—nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size can store today.
Approaching the limits
Over the decades, we have pushed the performance of our computers and our communications technology closer and closer to fundamental limits. The biggest change has been in the energy required for a single computation, which has dropped by 17 orders of magnitude since the 1940s, a factor of a hundred thousand trillion. But even with that big drop, we’re still a factor of several hundred thousand from the fundamental physical limit, set by information theory and the laws of thermo­dynamics. The largest gap exists for computational speed: Our current chips are some 35 orders of magnitude—that’s a 1 followed by 35 zeros—short of what quantum mechanics allows for a one-kilogram computer.
SOURCES: LLOYD (2000); BEKENSTEIN (1981); LANDAUER (1961); HOLEVO (1973); CAVES AND DRUMMOND (1994); BURKS (1947); BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; IEEE IRDS; NVIDIA; CISCO
The last limit is on communication—how fast information can be moved. Every wire and every fiber ultimately carries its signal on quanta, the indivisible packets (photons in the case of light) in which energy travels. In 1973, the Soviet mathematician Alexander Holevo determined the ultimate limit on how much information a stream of quanta can convey. A watt of light delivers only so many photons each second, and quantum mechanics fixes how many distinguishable ways they can arrive—how many messages a receiver could ever tell apart. A single channel carrying one watt, at the Holevo limit, could deliver on the order of 10
bits per second. Today’s optical links, or interconnects, deliver about one-millionth that rate for the same power. But the gap is narrowing quickly inside data centers, where each generation of interconnects is asked to move more bits on less power, spending less energy on the electronics and using light to cover more of the distance.
Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun.
The room that remains
The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter.
Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation.
In 1959, Richard Feynman offered a $1,000 prize to the first person to make a motor 1/64th of an inch on a side. William McLellan, a Caltech-trained engineer, soon fabricated one by hand under a microscope. This image shows an enlarged demonstration model (right).
GETTY IMAGES
Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined.
But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in.
This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat.
Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication.
Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet.
Between the floor and the ceiling
It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter.
But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
These gaps are invitations. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
For most of the last century, we proceeded down both paths together. We built more computers, and the computers themselves grew smaller and better. Now we mostly build more, and the ceiling is coming into view. A power grid can carry only so many gigawatts, and a region can spare only so much land and water. Yet every road map for what comes next is drawn from the same starting point: the machines we already have. Build more of them and you climb toward the ceiling; build better ones and you descend a little further, but only as far as the transistor’s own floor. There is a third direction. Start with a physics experiment operating at the floor and build up.
It has been done before. The transistor was a physics experiment before it was an industry; the laser was a laboratory curiosity before it carried the world’s conversations under the ocean; giant magnetoresistance went from physics discovery to the read head of every disk drive within a decade. In each case, the physics experiment came first and showed what was possible, and engineers then turned it into a machine that can be scaled up. Building the experiments that operate at these fundamental limits, and then scaling them up without losing that performance, is the work that remains. The next machines will not be reached by descent; they will be built from the bottom up. There
still plenty of room at the bottom.
Volkan Gurses
is a postdoctoral researcher at MIT and a visiting researcher at Nvidia. He received his PhD in electrical engineering from Caltech. He studies the fundamental physical limits of information technologies and builds integrated circuits and systems that approach those limits.

Dr. Ina Czyborra, Senatorin für Wissenschaft, Gesundheit und Pflege des Landes Berlin:
„Die Digitalisierung des Gesundheitswesens braucht qualifizierte Fachkräfte, die technologische Innovationen mit den Anforderungen einer guten Versorgung verbinden. Der neue duale Studiengang der HWR Berlin bringt Wissenschaft und Praxis zusammen und stärkt das Land Berlin als führender Gesundheits- und Wissenschaftsstandort. Er zeigt, wie wir durch gezielte Ausbildung, Wissenstransfer und enge Kooperationen die digitale Transformation gestalten und die Innovationskraft unserer Gesundheitswirtschaft nachhaltig sichern.“
Mit dem dualen Bachelorstudiengang BWL / Digitales Gesundheitsmanagement bietet die Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin (HWR Berlin) seit Oktober 2026 eine Ausbildung an der Schnittstelle von Management, Technologie und Gesundheitsversorgung. Die offizielle Eröffnungsfeier am 19. Oktober 2026 im KEH Evangelisches Krankenhaus Königin Elisabeth Herzberge, einem der ersten Praxispartner, bringt Vertreterinnen und Vertreter des Berliner Senats, der HWR Berlin, der Berliner Krankenhausgesellschaft (BKG), Praxispartner und die ersten Studierenden zusammen.
Prof. Dr. Jens Hermsdorf, Präsident der Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin:
„Wer Fachkräfte für morgen gewinnen will, muss Studium und Arbeitswelt enger zusammenbringen. Genau das leistet das vielfältige duale Studienangebot an der Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin seit mehr als 30 Jahren. Mit der neuen Fachrichtung BWL / Digitales Gesundheitsmanagement gehen wir jetzt einen Schritt weiter und verbinden Wirtschaft und Gesundheitssektor mit Digitalisierung für einen Studiengang, der hervorragend zu den Bedarfen und zu Berlin als Gesundheitsmetropole passt. Möglich wurde das mit der maßgeblichen Unterstützung der Berliner Krankenhausgesellschaft, den beteiligten Unternehmen aus der Gesundheitsbranche und der Senatsverwaltung für Wissenschaft, Gesundheit und Pflege. Ein gutes Beispiel dafür, was möglich ist, wenn Praxis, Hochschule und Politik gemeinsam an einem Ziel arbeiten.“
Marc Schreiner, Geschäftsführer der BKG Berliner Krankenhausgesellschaft:
„Berliner Krankenhäuser nehmen teilweise bei der Digitalisierung Spitzenplätze im Bundesvergleich ein. Mit dem neuen Studiengang setzen wir diesen Weg konsequent fort. BKG und HWR haben ihn gemeinsam mit den Krankenhäusern praxisnah entwickelt, für die Krankenhäuser und ihren konkreten Bedarf. So schaffen wir eine akademische Qualifizierung, die den digitalen Wandel in den Kliniken gezielt unterstützt und den Digitalisierungsreifegrad weiter erhöht. Die praktische Ausbildung in den Berliner Krankenhäusern verankert das theoretische Wissen unmittelbar in der Praxis. Die BKG bringt dabei ihre Erfahrung und ihre Rolle als Impulsgeberin für die organisationsbezogene Digitalisierung im Krankenhaus ein.“
Duale Praxispartnern für die digitale Transformation
Zu den ersten dualen Praxispartnern des Studiengangs zählen das BG Klinikum Unfallkrankenhaus Berlin, die Charité DFM Facility Management GmbH, das Digital-Health-Unternehmen samedi, die Non-Profit-Organisation Eurotransplant Deutschland, die Helios Kliniken, das EKS Evangelische Klinikum Berlin Südwest, das KEH Evangelisches Krankenhaus Königin Elisabeth Herzberge und die Sana & Sana IT Service GmbH.
Prof. Dr. Anna-Maria von Saucken, Studiengangsleiterin BWL / Digitales Gesundheitsmanagement der HWR Berlin:
„Digitalisierung im Gesundheitswesen beginnt nicht mit dem Kauf einer Software. Sie beginnt mit dem Verständnis dafür, wie Versorgung funktioniert und wie sich Arbeitsabläufe verbessern lassen. Deshalb verbinden wir betriebswirtschaftliche Inhalte mit technologischem Verständnis und Kenntnissen des Gesundheitswesens. Unsere Studierenden sollen digitale Veränderungen fachlich beurteilen und gemeinsam mit den Beschäftigten gestalten können.“
Management, Technologie und Gesundheitsversorgung verbinden
Im Studium geht es um die Verbindung von Management, Technologie und Gesundheitsversorgung. Neben digitalen Anwendungen stehen organisatorische Veränderungen und die Digitalisierung von Gesundheitsorganisationen auf dem Lehrplan. Ein besonderer Schwerpunkt liegt auf dem verantwortungsvollen Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz und auf Fragen der Mensch-Maschine-Interaktion.
Praxis von Anfang an
Der Studiengang ist als duales Studium konzipiert. Theoriephasen an der HWR Berlin wechseln sich mit mehrmonatigen Praxisphasen in Unternehmen und Organisationen des Gesundheitswesens ab. So sammeln die Studierenden bereits während des Studiums Berufserfahrung, arbeiten an realen Projekten mit und erhalten eine Vergütung.
Für den nächsten Durchgang sucht die HWR Berlin weitere Praxispartner. Insbesondere Krankenhäuser, Krankenkassen, Gesundheitsdienstleister, Digital-Health-Unternehmen und weitere Organisationen der Gesundheitswirtschaft können Studierende im dualen Studium als Praxispartner begleiten. Diese erhalten die Möglichkeit, qualifizierte Nachwuchskräfte frühzeitig zu gewinnen, sie gezielt weiterzuentwickeln und langfristig an die eigene Organisation zu binden.
Attraktive Perspektiven für Studieninteressierte
Der Studiengang eröffnet vielfältige berufliche Perspektiven im Gesundheitssektor. Absolventinnen und Absolventen können beispielsweise im Digitalisierungsmanagement von Krankenhäusern, bei Krankenkassen, in Health-Tech-Unternehmen oder in Projekten zur Entwicklung digitaler Gesundheitsangebote tätig werden.
Duales Studium an der HWR Berlin
Die Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin ist der größte Anbieter dualer Studiengänge in der Hauptstadtregion mit über 2.000 Studienplätzen in 20 Fachrichtungen aus Wirtschaft, Technik, IT, Recht und Öffentlichem Dienst. Seit über 30 Jahren arbeitet die HWR Berlin erfolgreich mit rund 700 Partnerunternehmen, Behörden und der Polizei Berlin zusammen und bietet rund 30 duale Bachelor- und Masterstudiengänge an. Übernahmequoten und Berufsaussichten für Absolventinnen und Absolventen dualer Studiengänge sind überdurchschnittlich gut.

Für die Berichterstattung vermitteln wir Journalist*innen gern passende Gesprächspartner*innen aus der HWR Berlin und von Praxispartnern.
Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin
Die Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht Berlin (HWR Berlin) ist eine fachlich breit aufgestellte, international ausgerichtete Hochschule für angewandte Wissenschaften, einer der bundesweit größten staatlichen Anbieter für das duale Studium und im akademischen Weiterbildungsbereich. Sie sichert den Fachkräftebedarf in der Hauptstadtregion und darüber hinaus. Rund 12 000 Studierende sind in über 60 Studiengängen der Wirtschafts-, Verwaltungs-, Rechts-, Ingenieur- und Polizei- und Sicherheitswissenschaften sowie in internationalen Master- und MBA-Studiengängen eingeschrieben. Die HWR Berlin ist die viertgrößte Hochschule für den öffentlichen Dienst in Deutschland und mehrfach prämierte Gründungshochschule. Über 700 Kooperationen mit Partnern in der Wirtschaft und im öffentlichen Dienst garantieren den ausgeprägten Praxisbezug in Lehre und Forschung. 195 aktive Partnerschaften mit Universitäten auf allen Kontinenten fördern einen regen Studierendenaustausch und die internationale Forschungszusammenarbeit. Die HWR Berlin ist Mitglied im Hochschulverbund „UAS7 – Alliance for Excellence“ und unterstützt die Initiative der Hochschulrektorenkonferenz „Weltoffene Hochschulen – Gegen Fremdenfeindlichkeit“.

Das vergleichsweise hohe Gewicht von Glasbehältern und der damit verbundene Energiebedarf bei Herstellung und Transport könnten sich dank einer gemeinsamen Material- und Technologieentwicklung der EXXOSQEL GmbH mit dem Fraunhofer-Institut für Silicatforschung ISC deutlich reduzieren lassen. Eine neuartige Oberflächenbehandlung erhöht die mechanische Belastbarkeit von Glasbehältern und schafft damit die Voraussetzung für dünnwandigere und leichtere Verpackungen auf Glasbasis. Eine Gewichtsreduktion von 15 % wurde bereits realisiert. Bei entsprechend angepasster und stabiler Heißformgebung halten die Entwicklungspartner künftig Gewichtsreduktionen von bis zu 40 % für technisch erreichbar.
Glas besitzt als Verpackungsmaterial zahlreiche Vorteile. Glasflaschen und andere Glasbehälter sind geschmacks- und geruchsneutral, geben keine Weichmacher oder Lösemittel ab, lassen sich in Mehrwegsystemen vielfach wieder befüllen oder können über das gut etablierte Glasrecycling als wertvoller Sekundärrohstoff energiesparend wieder in die Glasproduktion zurückgeführt werden. Sie haben also hervorragende Eigenschaften für die Verpackung von hochwertigen Produkten wie Lebensmittel, Medikamente oder Kosmetika und können sehr nachhaltig sein.
Ein wesentlicher Nachteil ist das im Vergleich zu Kunststoffbehältern oder mehrlagigen Papier-Metall-Kunststoff-Verbundverpackungen relativ hohe Gewicht und der hohe Energieverbrauch bei Produktion und Transport. Deshalb zielen aktuell viele Entwicklungen darauf, Glas dünner und gleichzeitig widerstandsfähiger zu machen. Dadurch lassen sich nicht nur Rohstoffe und Energie bei der Fertigung einsparen. Auch bei der Abfüllung und beim Transport wird weniger Energie benötigt. »Wie schaffen wir es angesichts der Anforderungen aus der Verpackungsverordnung , Glas bei gleicher Festigkeit leichter zu machen, damit Glasverpackungen im Wettbewerb mit anderen Verpackungsmaterialien bestehen können?«, umreißt Thomas Sauer von EXXOSQEL das Ziel der Entwicklung. Die Materialentwicklung kann dabei direkt zur Reduzierung des CO₂-Fußabdrucks von Glasbehältern beitragen.
Wie lässt sich die Bruchfestigkeit von Glas erhöhen?
Das hat fast jeder schon erlebt: Eine Glasflasche fällt auf den Boden und zerbricht in Stücke. Doch auch bei vergleichsweise kleinen Belastungen kann Glas bereits brechen. Dafür sind beispielsweise thermische Spannungen infolge schneller Temperaturänderungen oder Oberflächenfehler und Mikrorisse verantwortlich, die bei Produktion, Abfüllung oder Transport entstehen können. Auch unsachgemäße Handhabung im täglichen Gebrauch kann dazu führen.
Die im Flachglasbereich üblichen Verfahren der thermischen oder chemischen Härtung, die durch gezielt induzierte Druckspannungen in der oberflächennahen Glasschicht die Festigkeit erhöhen, sind in der Behälterglasindustrie teils aus technischen Gründen, teils aufgrund des Aufwands und der Kosten nicht verbreitet. In der Behälterglasindustrie etabliert sind jedoch Beschichtungen, die direkt nach der Heißformgebung (Hot-End-Coating, HEC, also Heißendvergütung) und nach dem Kühlofen (Cold-End-Coating, CEC, also Kaltendvergütung) aufgebracht werden. Für die USA gibt die American Glass Research den Anteil so behandelter Behältergläser mit über 95 % an. Die Heißendvergütung soll beispielsweise die Radien in den Mikrorissen vergrößern und die Adhäsion der Kaltendvergütung ermöglichen, während die Kaltendvergütung die Oberfläche gleitfähiger macht und damit den Verschleiß in der Abfüllung verringert. Für die Kaltendvergütung werden Beschichtungen auf Basis von Polyethylenwachsen eingesetzt. Bei Mehrwegflaschen wird die Kaltendvergütung durch die alkalische Flaschenwäsche bereits nach wenigen Umläufen weitgehend abgewaschen.
»Rissausheilung« durch eine neue Beschichtung
Mit der von EXXOSQEL und dem Fraunhofer-Institut für Silicatforschung ISC entwickelten Kombination aus neuem Beschichtungsmaterial und angepasster Beschichtungstechnologie werden Oberflächendefekte zu einem guten Teil überbrückt, gleichsam »geheilt«. »Konkret erzeugen wir bei der Synthese aus mehreren Komponenten ein dreidimensional vernetztes Komposit, dessen Matrix nach der Beschichtungsapplikation auf molekularer Ebene kovalente Brücken in den durch die Heißformgebung und Abkühlung entstandenen Mikrorissen bildet«, so Thomas Sauer, Geschäftsführer von EXXOSQEL. Dadurch erhöht sich die zum Bruch notwendige Energie erheblich. Laborversuche haben bereits deutliche Verbesserungen der Glasfestigkeit gezeigt. Bei nahezu allen bislang getesteten Glasbehältertypen erhöhte sich in Druck- und Schlagversuchen die bis zum Bruch ertragene Belastung erheblich. In Einzelfällen konnten die Behälter selbst bei der mit den Versuchsapparaturen maximal aufbringbaren Belastung von 10 Joule beziehungsweise 40 bar nicht mehr zum Bruch gebracht werden. Das Unternehmen schätzt, dass dünnere Glassubstrate Materialeinsatz, Energieverbrauch und CO₂-Emissionen senken könnten, indem sie Gewichtsreduzierungen von bis zu 40 % ermöglichen, sofern stabile Heißformgebungsprozesse sichergestellt werden können. Hinzu kommt, dass die Beschichtung eine geschlossene Oberfläche herstellt. Dadurch werden höhere Brillanz und bessere Haptik jeder Flasche erreicht. Außerdem entstehen geringere Reibungskräfte zwischen den Flaschen.
Vom Labormaßstab zum Prototyp
Die Zusammenarbeit zwischen EXXOSQEL und dem Fraunhofer ISC zielt auf die Marktreife des Produkts ab. EXXOSQEL entwickelt die Materialformulierung und stellt sie derzeit mit Unterstützung des Fraunhofer ISC im Labormaßstab her. Das Fraunhofer ISC bringt darüber hinaus seine Erfahrung bei der Hochskalierung von Materialsynthesen und Beschichtungstechnologien beim nächsten Schritt aus dem Labor- in den Technikumsmaßstab ein. Beide Partner arbeiten bei Materialformulierung und Technologieentwicklung eng zusammen. Auch die Skalierung der Beschichtung unterstützen die Würzburger Forscherinnen und Forscher: »Wir wollen die Anwendung der neuen Beschichtung so gestalten, dass sie leicht in bestehende Fertigungsprozesse integriert werden kann«, unterstreicht Dr. Ferdinand Somorowsky, Leiter der Beschichtungstechnologie am Fraunhofer ISC, den Anwendungsaspekt. Gemeinsam arbeiten die Forschungspartner nun am nächsten Skalierungsschritt, erklärt Thomas Sauer: »Wir beherrschen den Versuchsaufbau im Labor. Für 2027 planen wir den Aufbau eines Technikums, in dem wir sowohl die Herstellung der Beschichtungslösung als auch die Applikationstechnik weiter skalieren. Damit wollen wir die Voraussetzungen für eine industrienahe Validierung und den nächsten Schritt in Richtung industrieller Serienfertigung schaffen. In den nächsten Schritten werden wir dafür Partner aus der Behälterglas-, Getränke- und Lebensmittelindustrie sowie aus dem Maschinen- und Anlagenbau einbinden.«

Solarglas wird als transparenter Witterungsschutz und Trägermaterial für Photovoltaikmodule eingesetzt. Eine von EXXERGY entwickelte Beschichtungstechnologie zielt darauf, die Materialfestigkeit von Solarglas so weit zu erhöhen, dass deutlich dünnere Scheiben möglich werden. Unter Beibehaltung der mechanischen Eigenschaften ließe sich die Glasmasse um bis zu 40 % reduzieren. Gemeinsam mit dem Fraunhofer-Institut für Silicatforschung ISC wird das Verfahren weiter hochskaliert. Auf der Glasstec 2026 präsentiert die EXXERGY-Tochter EXXOSQEL einen Demonstrator aus der gemeinsamen Entwicklung in Halle 11 an Stand E12.
Der Ausbau der Photovoltaik ist ein wesentlicher Baustein der Energiewende. Gleichzeitig werden auch für die Herstellung von PV-Modulen erhebliche Mengen an Rohstoffen und Energie benötigt. Einen erheblichen Anteil daran hat das eisenarme Solarglas, das die Zellen und die elektrisch leitenden Komponenten im Modul vor Witterungseinflüssen schützt und zugleich eine hohe Lichttransmission gewährleisten muss. Auch die Stabilitätsanforderungen bei großflächigen PV-Modulen sind anspruchsvoll. Je nach Bauweise und mechanischen Anforderungen liegt die Flächenmasse heutiger PV-Module typischerweise im Bereich von etwa 11 bis 13 kg/m²; besonders robust ausgelegte Module können Werte bis etwa 16 kg/m² erreichen. Das verbraucht Ressourcen, verursacht Transportkosten und für die Montage sind entsprechend massive Unterkonstruktionen notwendig. »Weniger Glas« bedeutet deshalb weniger Materialeinsatz und Prozessenergie sowie ein geringeres Gewicht bei Transport und Montage.
Dünn, aber stabil?
Ein möglicher Lösungsansatz besteht darin, dünneres Glas für Solarmodule zu verwenden. Mit einem Gewichtsanteil von 70 bis 80 % ist Glas bei heutigen PV-Modulen eine der wichtigsten Stellschrauben in Bezug auf Materialeinsatz und Modulgewicht. Eine Reduktion der Glasstärke spart entsprechend Gewicht und Ressourcen bei der Herstellung sowie bei Transport und Montage. Darüber hinaus wird weniger Energie bei der Herstellung verbraucht. Die Herausforderung besteht darin, die Festigkeit des Glases so weit zu erhöhen, dass auch dünne Glasscheiben stabil genug gegen Hagel, Schnee- und Windlast sind.
Thermische Vorspannung stößt bei dünnem Glas an Grenzen
Ein Standardverfahren für die Erhöhung der Stabilität und Bruchfestigkeit bei Flachglas ist die thermische Vorspannung. Ein durch Anblasen mit kalter Luft gesteuertes Abkühlen im Produktionsprozess führt zu einer definierten thermischen Vorspannung. Dabei entstehen Druckspannungen an der Oberfläche, die das Wachstum von Rissen erschweren. Das Glas wird bruchfester. So behandeltes Glas wird beispielsweise als »Einscheiben-Sicherheitsglas« (ESG) als Architekturglas, im Automobilbau oder in der Möbelindustrie eingesetzt. Bei Solarglas ist 3,2 mm eine gängige Nennstärke; eine weitere Reduktion auf 2 mm und darunter lässt sich mit konventioneller thermischer Vorspannung jedoch nur eingeschränkt, wenn überhaupt realisieren.
Ein weiteres Vorspannungsverfahren, das vor allem bei dünnem Glas eingesetzt werden kann, ist die sogenannte chemische Härtung. Hier wird die Oberflächenspannung auf chemischem Weg durch Ionenaustausch an der Glasoberfläche erzielt, bei dem Natriumionen durch Kaliumionen ersetzt werden. Dadurch werden hohe Druckspannungen in der oberflächennahen Glasschicht erzeugt. Ein Vorteil dabei ist, dass weniger optische Verzerrungen als bei einer thermischen Vorspannung entstehen. Das Verfahren ist jedoch relativ aufwändig, energie- und zeitintensiv und für den großflächigen Einsatz nur eingeschränkt einsetzbar.
Rissausheilung durch neue Beschichtung
Da herstellungsbedingte Mikrorisse bei Flachglas eine entscheidende Rolle für die Glasfestigkeit spielen, setzt hier auch das neue Verfahren von EXXERGY und der für die Industrialisierung und Vermarktung des Verfahrens ausgegründete EXXOSQEL GmbH an. Mit einer Kombination von neuem Beschichtungsmaterial und angepasstem Applikationsverfahren können Oberflächendefekte nicht nur überdeckt, sondern teilweise gleichsam ausgeheilt werden. »Konkret erzeugen wir aus mehreren Komponenten ein dreidimensional vernetztes Komposit, dessen Matrix nach der Beschichtungsapplikation auf molekularer Ebene kovalente Brücken in den Mikrorissen bildet«, so Thomas Sauer, Geschäftsführer von EXXOSQEL. Dadurch erhöhe sich die zum Bruch notwendige Energie erheblich. Laborversuche hätten bereits deutliche Verbesserungen der Glasfestigkeit gezeigt: Nach mehreren iterativen Verbesserungen in den Rezepturen und Verfahren konnte die Festigkeit bei 2 mm dicken Glasproben um einen Faktor von bis zu 4 gesteigert werden, bei 1 mm dicken Glasproben sogar um einen Faktor von bis zu 7, jeweils gerechnet gegenüber einer nicht vorgespannten Referenz. Das Unternehmen schätzt, dass dünnere Glassubstrate Materialeinsatz und Energieverbrauch sowie CO₂-Emissionen deutlich senken könnten. Eine Reduktion der Glasmasse um bis zu 40 % könnte – je nach Modulaufbau – die Gesamtmasse des Moduls um rund 30 % verringern. Bei einem schweren Modul mit beispielsweise 16 kg/m² entspräche dies einer Reduktion auf rund 11 kg/m². Auch die Unterkonstruktionen könnten dadurch wegen der geringeren statischen Lasten entsprechend leichter ausgelegt werden.
Vom Labormaßstab zum Prototyp
Die nächsten Entwicklungsschritte zielen auf die Übertragung der Technologie von kleinen Glasproben auf größere Formate und schließlich auf Solarmodule in kommerzieller Größe. Die Material- und Beschichtungsentwicklung wurde bislang überwiegend von EXXERGY in enger Zusammenarbeit mit dem Fraunhofer ISC durchgeführt. »Die Schritte vom Labormuster bis zum großen Solarmodul erfordern viel Knowhow beim Hochskalieren der Materialsynthesen, der Applikationstechnik und der Modulfertigung«, so Thomas Sauer. Das Fraunhofer ISC bringt seine Erfahrung bei Synthesen bis zum 100-Liter-Maßstab und bei der Beschichtungsapplikation ein. Hier arbeiten beide Partner eng zusammen an Materialformulierung und Technologieentwicklung. Auch die Automatisierung der Beschichtung unterstützen die Würzburger Forscherinnen und Forscher: »Wir wollen die Anwendung der neuen Beschichtung so gestalten, dass sie leicht in bestehende Fertigungsprozesse integriert werden kann«, unterstreicht Dr. Ferdinand Somorowsky, Leiter der Beschichtungstechnologie am Fraunhofer ISC, den Anwendungsaspekt. Für die Übertragung auf Modulformate und die Prüfung größerer Formate arbeitet EXXERGY zudem mit dem Fraunhofer-Center für Silizium-Photovoltaik CSP in Halle zusammen. Gemeinsam treiben die Partner nun den nächsten Skalierungsschritt voran. Was das bedeutet, erklärt Thomas Sauer: »Wir sind mit unserer Beschichtungsentwicklung für Flachglas inzwischen in Richtung TRL 6 auf der international gebräuchlichen Skala des Technology Readiness Level unterwegs. Das heißt, wir haben erste Prototypen im Normmaß bereits erfolgreich unter praxisnahen Bedingungen hergestellt, die Belastungs-tests laufen derzeit. Mit dem nächsten Entwicklungsschritt zielen wir auf TRL 7 und damit auf die tatsächliche Einsatzumgebung.« EXXOSQEL bereitet die nächsten Schritte hinsichtlich Industrialisierung und Vermarktung vor.
Projektinformation
Die bisherigen Arbeiten wurden unter anderem in den Projekten Green Solar Modules (Förderkennzeichen 03EE1161E) und Green Solar Modules Glass II (Förderkennzeichen 03EEM1003) vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördert sowie durch das Unternehmen EXXERGY, einer mit der EXXOSQEL GmbH verbundenen Gesellschaft, finanziert.

title: Forschungstransfer im Fokus: Mehr als 120 KI-Talente und Expert:innen beim AI Grid Summit in Berlin
content:
Forschungstransfer im Fokus: Mehr als 120 KI-Talente und Expert:innen beim AI Grid Summit in Berlin

Von links nach rechts: Dr. Aljoscha Burchardt, DFKI, Dr. Tina Klüwer, AI Nation, Dr. Susanne Perner, TU Berlin, Jakob Haardt, EURICE, und Prof. Dr. Dr. Wolfgang Wahlster, AI Grid und DFKI.
